# THE PRESENT STATE
### O F  T H E
## ANABAPTISTS <term>Doopsgezinden: Literally "baptism-minded," the traditional Dutch name for Mennonites, emphasizing their belief in adult baptism rather than infant baptism.</term>
### O R
## MENNONITES,
### I N  T H E
## UNITED NETHERLANDS;
Following which is an ACCOUNT of the
## RHIJNSBURGERS
### O R
## COLLEGIANTS: <note>The Collegiants were a 17th-century Dutch religious group that valued individual interpretation of the Bible and met in "colleges" without formal clergy or creed.</note>
Both serving to show the Doctrine, External Condition, and Religious Practices of these Ecclesiastical Societies; together with a narrative concerning the Origin and Progress of the recent Disputes of the first-mentioned <note>referring to the Mennonites</note>, with the Teachers of the Reformed Church.

_Written in High German by Mr._
## SIMEON FREDERIK RUES.
_Translated and enlarged with notes for the clarification of certain details._

# PREFACE
### BY THE
## AUTHOR.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'I' containing the letter 'I' surrounded by floral flourishes and scrolls.</image-desc>I have spent the greater part of the time of my stay in the United Netherlands <note>The United Netherlands, or the Dutch Republic (1581–1795), was a confederation known for its relative religious tolerance and economic power.</note> in obtaining a well-founded and accurate understanding of the Present State of the Two Church Societies <note>The term "Church Societies" (original: *Kerkelyke Gezelschappen*) refers here to specific religious denominations or denominations.</note>, whose names are found on the title of this my little work <note>The author uses the diminutive *Werksken* (little work) as a gesture of modesty common in 18th-century literature.</note>, and who have established themselves especially in that respectable and powerful part of Europe. The knowledge and interaction which I have maintained with many prominent members of these Congregations has provided me with the useful means to successfully reach my objective (*). I have had the opportunity not only to learn the opinion and sentiment of these Churches on every point through private interaction with their Teachers <note>In this context, "Teachers" (*Leeraers*) refers to the ministers, pastors, or clergy of the denominations.</note> and other prominent Members; but at the same time I have also viewed most of their Religious Services <note>The original Dutch term *Godsdienstoeffeningen* literally translates to "religious exercises," encompassing liturgy, prayer, and preaching.</note> themselves, and heard their Public Orations. I have not relied upon the report of a single man, whether it concerned matters affecting his own denomination, or whether they were such that

---

(*) Namely, as much as one who is not a Native <note>The author uses *Inboorling* to clarify that while he is an outsider, he has been as thorough as a foreigner possibly can be.</note> could have done.

-># PREFACE<-

belonged to a different Society: no; I have questioned several persons of differing viewpoints regarding one and the same matter; and only then believed myself to know a thing with certainty, when I found opposing parties to be in agreement. In general, I have turned to such people from whom I could expect an accurate and thorough knowledge concerning what I sought to learn; and who, so it seemed to me, could gain no advantage from providing false or contradictory accounts. Similarly, public testimonies given before the eyes of an entire assembly have served me as a pure source of knowledge in these matters. And where certainty depended upon written reports, I have not neglected the opportunities to obtain them. In a word; I imagine and am confident that I have observed the duties of Circumspection and Sincerity in the best possible manner (*).

I trust that it will not be unpleasant for my fellow countrymen <note>original: *Landsgenooten*</note> if I openly share with them the reports which I have obtained in this way, both regarding the Mennonite <note>original: *Doopsgezinde*</note> Congregations and the Collegiants <note>The Collegiants were a 17th-century Dutch religious movement that grew out of Remonstrant circles; they met in "colleges" to discuss scripture without formal clergy or creedal requirements.</note>. For the Congregations of which I speak here constitute a quite considerable portion of the Churches, which

->### FROM THE AUTHOR.<-
<center>* 3</center>

have withdrawn themselves in these lands from the Roman Church-authority <note>original: *Roomsche Kerkhoofdigheit*; a reference to the Papacy and the Roman Catholic hierarchy</note>: they therefore deserve the notice of everyone who takes an interest in knowing the current state of foreign congregations. In the meantime, the information that has been set down generally abroad—and if I dare say it, also in the Netherlands themselves—regarding this matter is in many respects very confused, contradictory, and deficient. The blame for which must not be laid so much on foreigners, as on the inhabitants of these lands themselves; who, for various reasons, do not take the trouble to describe the state of these church communities in detail, or to publish the little that comes to light in Dutch—a language which the majority of foreign scholars do not master. I hope, therefore, that this work of mine will not be regarded as entirely superfluous or useless; but rather that it will perform a significant and desired service to all who have a desire to know the particular state and the various types of Christian denominations <note>original: *Gezindheden*</note> from close by, and to pass a well-founded judgment upon them.

However, I have not composed this treatise in the style of polemics <note>original: *Twistredenen*, meaning argumentative or controversial religious debates</note>, but in a historical manner; that is to say, I have [not] the foundations of the Church to which I profess (*),

---

(*) Mr. *Rues* is of the Brethren of the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530</note>, or as he most often calls them, the Evangelical-Lutherans.

not adduced <note>The text continues from the previous page: "I have [not] the foundation..."</note>, in order to set them against the opinions of these congregations that differ from them; and so I have likewise left out the objections by which these latter groups attempt to lend weight to their particular doctrines <note>original: *Leerstellingen*; refers to the specific dogmas or tenets of faith held by different sects</note>. If something of that sort has flowed in here or there, it happens only incidentally and in passing. If one wished to do this extensively, one would have to write a large book; and I would have undertaken a work that has been partially performed here and there already before my time.

Just as little has it been my aim to compile a complete history <note>original: *Geschiedenis*</note> of these congregations, from their origin up to these present times. This labor is indeed good and necessary; but it requires more time than I have, and very many resources: while it is nearly impossible to share something complete in this regard. I fairly leave this undertaking to two men well known to me who belong to these ecclesiastical societies, and who have already actually begun that work; and I doubt not at all that the learned world will reward their diligence with much gratitude, if they provide a thorough report on these important matters.

My objective has been to describe the condition <note>original: *Toestand*; meaning the current status or "state of affairs"</note> of these congregations as they appear in the present time, and specifically only in relation to the United Netherlands <note>original: *Vereenigde Nederlanden*; the Dutch Republic as it existed before the Napoleonic era</note>. And when I [do] this so clearly and consist- <note>The catchword "ftig" at the bottom of the page indicates the next page begins with "ently" (completing the word *overeenkomstig*).</note>

# FROM THE AUTHOR
->VII<-

...if I have been able to represent it as clearly as the investigation of it was difficult and arduous for me, I shall have done all that I intended. If anything has been brought forward here for the general benefit, it will richly reward my spent time and patience.

The disputes which have arisen between certain Anabaptists <term>Doopsgezinden; specifically the Dutch Mennonites or "Baptist-minded" groups who practiced adult baptism</term> and prominent theologians <term>Godgeleerden</term> of the Reformed Church <term>Gereformeerde Kerk; the state-supported Calvinist church in the Dutch Republic</term> of these lands, I have described in such a manner that I pray the much-honored reader to regard those passages of my little work—which seem to contain some judgment either of the matter itself, or of the origin and prospects, as well as the manner in which this struggle has been continued—not so much as my own thoughts, but rather as the opinion of other eminent and learned men in this province whom I have had the honor to consult on this subject. I have enjoyed the company of the prominent persons who have taken up the pen on both sides, and have enjoyed their worthy kindness; and I am in no way inclined to speak ill of anyone in particular. Nevertheless, I have had to fulfill the duty of a historian <term>Geschiedschryver</term>; and therefore have generally wished to recount, without partisanship, not only what has happened, but also what people judged of it. I wish with all my heart that all those who contend with one another on the grounds of faith might be united in the Truth <note>original: *Waerheit*</note> and the Faith <note>original: *Geloove*</note>! He who knows me will give me the testimony that I

# PREFACE BY THE AUTHOR.
->VIII<-

...[united in the Truth <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "...might be united in the Truth, and that I..."</note>] indeed highly esteem, zealously recommend, and promote external Civil tolerance, and even, in its proper measure, Christian tolerance. However, by contrast, I confine Ecclesiastical Tolerance <term>Kerkelyke Verdraegzaemheit; the degree to which a specific church body allows differing opinions within its own membership, as opposed to civil rights in society</term> within significantly narrower boundaries than many might wish. I am accustomed to doing no injustice either to the Truth itself or to Ecclesiastical Unity, which is founded upon a single shared understanding of that Truth. Furthermore, those who combat Errors <term>Dwalingen; theological mistakes or heresies</term> may be assured that I honor their zeal and earnestness and consider them praiseworthy to the best of my ability. Suppose, then, that under such circumstances I do not always judge one specific method or another of serving the Truth to be the most suitable or best; for that reason, I by no means deserve to be seen as a friend or defender of Error, nor as an opponent of the Protectors of the Truth.

May the LORD my GOD cause this humble work of mine to serve the advancement of the Truth and the glorification of His Name! Given at Leiden [in Holland], July 26, 1742.

<meta>catchword: VOOR-</meta>

## OF THE
# TRANSLATOR.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' featuring a figure seated in a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>This little work sees the light in our *Low-German language* <note>original: "Nederduitsche Tael"; at this time, this was the standard term for the Dutch language</note>, because it was believed that enough eager readers would be found for it among our *Countrymen*: seeing as no one until now has treated this subject so extensively and accurately. When I began translating it, I thought to add only very few and short *Notes* in some few places: but in the course of it I found reason to change my mind, and more extensive *Notes* were necessary here and there. Whether this PRESENT STATE OF THE MENNONITES <term>Tegenwoordige Staet der Doopsgezinden; the title of the book, referring to the "Doopsgezinden" or Mennonites, a group of Anabaptist Christians</term> is improved or disadvantaged by this, is for the Reader to judge.

I do not doubt that people in general will gladly want to do justice to the *Author*, that he (who is a *Lutheran Theologian* in *Germany*, and during his stay here in this country has done much research on this matter) describes things throughout with *Modesty* <note>original: "Bescheidenheit"; in this context, it implies impartiality, discretion, and a lack of sectarian bias</note>. # PREFACE

ever it is, one might say, naturally characteristic of all men, however much they are on their guard, to occasionally make a misstep in this regard. If it appeared to me that *Mr. Rues* <note>Simeon Friedrich Rues, the German author of the original work</note> was in this situation here or there, I have taken the liberty of noting it in a manner that I trust his Reverence <note>original: "zyn Eerw."; a formal honorific for a member of the clergy</note> himself will approve of.

In two or three places, it seemed to me that the *Circumspection* <note>original: "Omzigtigheid"; meaning caution or discretion in handling sensitive topics</note>, which generally accompanies the Author’s pen quite well and which is absolutely necessary in the *Relating of Theological Differences*, was not as successfully observed as I believed could have been done without violating the *Truth*. A word, a turn of phrase, might—through a common human weakness—render even otherwise truth-loving souls less attentive or inclined to notice what one would have liked them to observe. I therefore deemed it best to use my own wording in those places instead of the Author’s. Yet I pointed this out in the footnotes <note>original: "onder de Bladzyden"; literally "under the pages"</note>, and say it here once more, so that my faithfulness in translation may not be doubted.

It seemed to me that the **APPENDIX** <note>original: "Aenhangsel"</note> belonged immediately after the **STATE OF THE MENNONITES** <term>Staet der Doopsgezinden; the main subject of the book</term>. The Author has it at the very end in the original; perhaps because he only decided to compile it after the *Account of the Rijnsburgers* <note>The Rijnsburgers, also known as Collegiants, were a Dutch religious group with close ties to the Mennonites, known for their meetings in the town of Rijnsburg</note> had already begun to be printed. **THE PRESENT STATE**

# FROM THE TRANSLATOR

The account **OF THE COLLEGIANTS** <note>A Dutch spiritualist group known for their "colleges" or open meetings where any member could speak; they were closely linked with the Mennonites</note>, *which is the Fourth Chapter in Mr. Rues’ work* <note>Simeon Friedrich Rues, the original German author</note>, *I have added at the end as a separate piece, and have omitted the account found in "The Present State of the Netherlands"* <term>Tegenwoordigen Staet der Nederlanden; a popular contemporary encyclopedia of Dutch geography and history</term>, *which he had placed at the beginning; because anyone who wishes to do so can find it in that book. Regarding what the Author says about these people, I judged it best not to add any notes of any significance; but I have omitted one or two details in which the Author was either very poorly informed or with which it was best not to bore and delay the reader. Please be so kind as to favorably correct any printing errors <term>Drukfeilen; literally "press-failings"</term> that have crept in; meanwhile, may my fellow countrymen find an honest pastime and useful education through reading this fruit of my leisure* <note>original: "vrugt myner onlede"; literally "fruit of my non-idleness," referring to the work produced during the translator's spare time away from his primary duties</note>!

->From my chamber, the<-
->11 December 1744.<-

## APPENDIX;

<margin>Concerning the Name of the Baptism-minded.</margin>
The coreligionists, who in Germany and elsewhere are called *Anabaptists* <note>original: "Wederdoopers" — literally "re-baptizers," a term often used by critics to imply they were repeating a sacrament already performed in infancy.</note> or *Anabaptists*, are known in the United Netherlands by the name of BAPTISM-MINDED; by which one refers to People who, regarding the matter of Infant Baptism, hold particular views. They also bear the name of MENNONITES or *Mennonists*, after *Menno Simons*, a Man who did an uncommon amount for the building up of these Congregations: although there are many among them who entirely disapprove of this naming. My intention is by no means to compile a History of these Congregations, which from their very first Origin until the Pres-

<margin>Concerning their Origin, as they themselves relate it.</margin>
The Baptism-minded <note>original: "Doopsgezinden" — The Dutch term for Mennonites, focusing on their belief in adult baptism.</note> themselves claim that their Ancestors were true Descendants of the *Waldensians* <note>A pre-Reformation movement of "Poor Men" who sought to return to the simple poverty of the early church.</note>, who, on account of the heavy Persecutions with which they were oppressed, fled to various regions of Europe, and there, while retaining both their Old Doctrine and partially also their well-ordered Church Government and Discipline, held their ground until the times of the *Reformation* <note>original: "Geloofshervorminge" — literally "Faith-reformation."</note>. They add to this that these Congregations, in the times of the blessed *Reformation*, were so encouraged that they stepped somewhat into the light of day, and took a greater liberty in the Public Practice of their Religion.

However, seeing that at the same time many rebels and visionaries in Germany took part first in the notorious Peasants' War <note>original: "Boerenkryg" — a massive social and religious uprising (1524–1525).</note> and subsequently in the Münster Rebellion <note>original: "Munstersche Oproer" — a radical and violent attempt to establish a "New Jerusalem" in the city of Münster (1534–1535).</note>, who among other things maintained the Re-baptism <note>original: "Wederdoop"</note> of those who had been baptized in their Infancy; this gave the High Authorities cause to be greatly inflamed against all those who rejected Infant Baptism <note>original: "Kinderdoop"</note>: since they made this unfounded conclusion, that all who in respect to the latter agreed in some measure with *Müntzer's* <note>original: "Muntzerus" — referring to Thomas Müntzer, a radical reformer during the Peasants' War.</note> Followers and the *Anabaptists* <note>original: "Wederdoopers"</note> of *Münster*, must also be of the same nature in other matters, or even entirely from their gang, and therefore ill-disposed toward the General Welfare.

And the High Authorities would have been further strengthened in this opinion because the Innocent and Quiet Baptism-minded <note>original: "Doopsgezinden" — The Dutch term for Mennonites, focusing on their belief in adult baptism.</note> spoke against the Swearing of Oaths, and judged the Office of Authority <note>Holding government or military office, which Mennonites traditionally refused.</note> differently than is common. From this it arose that these innocent and defenseless *Waldensian Baptism-minded* <note>original: "Waldenzer Doopsgezinden" — referring to the claim that they descended from the medieval Waldensian movement.</note> were dealt with according to the harsh Edicts <note>original: "Plakaten" — official decrees or proclamations issued by the government.</note> which had been issued against the rebellious and warring Anabaptists, and especially those of Münster <note>A radical group that took over the city of Münster in the 1530s, leading to a violent siege; their actions caused a long-lasting stigma against all who practiced adult baptism.</note>, without properly observing the extraordinarily large difference that existed between those two parties. And this was also said to be the reason why the Authors of Church Histories imprudently mixed them together. Finally, as they add, after much innocent blood had been shed, the Authorities became fully convinced that the Beliefs and Conduct of the Baptism-minded were of an entirely different nature than the old Doctrine and Aims of the Rebellious Anabaptists, and gradually became more lenient; while the Historians, for lack of better information, persisted in the old misconception until almost the present day.

<margin>As others relate it.</margin>
But from the other side, these are the thoughts commonly held. Against this sort of people, it is argued, the authorities acted with every right according to the well-known strict laws, and they were tolerated nowhere. Concerning their Schisms, or Divisions.
</margin>
Now when the Baptism-minded <note>The Dutch term is "Doopsgezinden," the name preferred by the Mennonites to distinguish themselves from radical "Anabaptists."</note> had finally brought their affairs this far, they experienced what had happened to many other religious groups: namely, that while they enjoyed peace from the outside, they frequently fell into unrest from within, which commonly resulted in Schisms or Divisions. And there is no reason to wonder at this, as if it were something extraordinary, when one observes the condition of these congregations with any degree of accuracy. People who at that time still tolerated little Scholarship <note>Early Mennonites often viewed formal academic theology with suspicion, prioritizing "simple" faith and biblical literalism.</note>, and moreover knew neither how to form nor how to maintain definite and fixed concepts; People who had not established among themselves a Church Order <term>Church Order (Kerkordening): A set of rules or a constitution governing the practices and discipline of a church.</term> suitable for all circumstances, but rather proceeded only as each incident arose, according to their best thoughts which they formed in such circumstances, and desired others to have acted in the same way; People who could survey neither the Doctrine of Faith and Life and its entire scope, nor every part thereof according to its particular weight and importance, nor the nature of men in general, nor the Nature and Requirements of a well-established Society in its full extent, but instead viewed occurring matters only from their own narrow viewpoints, and wished them to be viewed by others in the same way; People, finally, who were of the mind that everyone without distinction was unyieldingly obliged to follow their own so-called good opinion and conviction: such People, I say, could not possibly remain united with one another for a long time, nor live in complete confidence, as soon as they were merely of

For it is this alone that binds intolerant spirits together, and can focus their otherwise very different thoughts and insights on such things in which they have more in common; that is, on the **Common Complaints** against the **Enemies** and **Persecutors**, on the asserting and praising of **Christian Tolerance**, on **Means of Common Maintenance**, and the like.

The **Desire for Honor** and **Self-Will** <note>original: "Eigen Goeddunken" — A term often used in theological texts to describe the stubborn adherence to one's own opinion over communal or scriptural authority.</note> seek to gain ground, both in matters of Religion and of the Church as well as in temporal and earthly affairs: although they know how to cover themselves in the former under a plausible cloak, and to disguise themselves with fine names and pretenses in such a way that they blind and deceive even those whom they obviously rule. When one has grown weary of fighting with public Opponents, or has rest from them; when there seems to be nothing more to do from that side, and consequently spiritual **Ambition** under the guise of **Zeal for Truth** sees no more field open for itself on that side; then it turns toward the internal structure of its Church, and will—under the pretense of the **Restoration** of things that have fallen, or **Improvement** of newly beneficial things—not so much provide for the best of the Church, but rather attempt to draw the eyes, the high esteem, and the praise of men toward itself. **Self-Will**, the faithful companion of **Ambition**, helps and supports it, in such cases, with all its strength *.

From this time onward, there were two kinds of **Mennonites**: namely, the *Coarse*, that is the Moderate, to whom the mocking nickname of *Muck-carts* was given; and the *Fine*, or the **Strict Mennonites**. The congregations in other provinces that agreed with the former also received the name of **Waterlanders**, and were treated as such by the rest, regardless of where they lived or from which land they may have originated.

This dispute ended in the cutting off of fellowship and in the **Ban** <note>The practice of excommunication and social shunning used to maintain the purity of the religious community.</note>. After two parties had emerged from a single one, the schism became all the more noticeable because the divided groups were, besides this matter, somewhat distinguished from each other in external things. The *Frisians* kept themselves simple in their clothing; but were quite neat and tidy regarding their linens and houses. The *Flemish*, quite the opposite, kept their household furnishings plain; but in their clothing, they were more outward <note>This refers to the "Flemish" tendency at the time to wear more expensive or fashionable fabrics compared to the austere Frisians.</note>. Seeing as other congregations in the **United Netherlands** were also entangled in this struggle, and they had to choose a side if they did not wish to be rejected and hated by both; so those who held with the *Flemish* were from that time called the *Flemish* congregation, while the rest were called the *Frisian* congregation. The *Waterlanders*, who gradually became more and more moderate in all matters, recognized both the other parties as their brothers; yet they were hated as much by the one as by the other: and those two societies believed that each alone constituted the true **Church of Christ** on earth. Furthermore, **High Germans** <note>original: "Hoogduitschen" — Mennonites originating from German-speaking lands who immigrated to the Netherlands.</note>, or **Mennonites** from Germany, had settled in the United Netherlands: these were likewise separated from the church fellowship of the locals, partly because of their language and partly because of certain specific views. <margin>Of the Fine, or Old Flemish.</margin>
Those of the *Old Sort* have since constituted a significantly smaller number than the Moderate or Tolerant. But they are still one of the main branches of the **Mennonites** <note>original: "Doopsgezinden" — literally 'baptism-minded,' the common Dutch term for Mennonites.</note> today; and they are now called not so much the *Fine* <note>original: "Fynen" — a nickname for the stricter groups who were "refined" or "purified" in their conduct.</note>, as commonly and generally the *Old Flemish*; without one strictly observing whether, with regard to the above-mentioned first **Schism** <note>original: "Scheuring"</note>, they are actually *Old Frisians* or *Old Flemish* among themselves. They are divided into various parties to this day: of which one will not extend the hand of brotherhood to the other. Their two main types are the so-called *Danzigers* and *Groningers*. They have many things to bring against each other; and each party wants to be the *Finest*. Yet however modest and simple they both may be; they are nevertheless held to be worldly and all too outward by the *Finest of All*.

<margin>Of the Main Branch of the Coarse or Tolerant.</margin>
On the other hand, from the aforementioned times, one found the second main party of the **Mennonites**, which were called the *Coarse* <note>original: "Grooven" — a nickname for the more liberal or moderate groups, implying they were less "refined" in their application of church discipline.</note>, that is the Moderate or Tolerant; and who have distinguished themselves significantly from the *Fine* with regard to Doctrine, to **Church Discipline** <note>original: "Kerktugt"</note>, and to outward Manners, as well as in many other things. These first consisted of Waterlander, thereafter also of Frisian, and finally also of Flemish congregations; and together they made up a disproportionately larger and more distinguished group than the above-mentioned *Old Sort*. Their Wealth, which they easily acquired through Trade <note>original: "Koophandel"</note>, combined with their moderate and frugal way of living; their frequent Interaction with other people, which naturally arose from commerce and made their manners more accommodating; as well as the Love for the Sciences <note>original: "Wetenschappen" — referring here to academic study and higher learning</note>, which took root among many of them, provided a desirable occasion for this transition everywhere. Meanwhile, regardless of this, one can very easily realize that these Tolerant Societies <note>original: "Verdraegzaeme Genootschappen"</note>, since they had arisen from different Parent Congregations <note>original: "Stamgemeenten" — literally 'stem' or 'root' communities</note> at different times and from varying perspectives, could in no way have perfectly agreed with one another. Therefore, they also remained for a long time everywhere on their own and separate; indeed, they did not have the best opinions of each other. Because of this, one could find so many small Congregations <note>original: "Gemeenten"</note> living independently, not only throughout the country in general but even within single locations. Furthermore, across an entire province, they stood in no close Connection with each other, even in cases where they shared the same Name, Custom, and Institutions. I shall mention in the SECOND CHAPTER <note>original: "TWEEDE HOOFTSTUK"</note> of this Treatise how the [three] different sorts of Moderate Mennonites <note>original: "Gematigde Doopsgezinden"</note> were partly united, and into which Special Brotherhoods they are still divided today.

<margin>
I. *Of the Doctrine of the Old Flemings.*
1. *They hold to the Confessions.*
</margin>

**T**he Old Flemings <note>The Old Flemings (Oude Vlamingen) were a subgroup of Mennonites known for their strict adherence to traditional practices and rigorous church discipline.</note> (to begin with the **DOCTRINE**,) first agree with one another in this: that they hold fast to the Old *Confessions of Faith*, which were drawn up among the Mennonites in the sixteenth and following centuries. For this reason, they do not grant their **Members** such an unlimited freedom of teaching and believing as a large portion of the Mennonites—of whom I shall speak hereafter—is accustomed to do.

<margin>
2. *They follow Menno Simons.*
</margin>

They are, *Secondly*, in respect to the Doctrine of Faith, the true and unchanging followers of *Menno Simons* <note>Menno Simons (1496–1561) was the Frisian priest who became a leader of the Anabaptist movement; his followers were named Mennonites.</note>, and gladly bear the name of **MENNONITES** after that man: whereas a large part of the Mennonites wants to hear or know nothing of him.

</margin>

<margin>4. Of the Humanity [of Christ].</margin>
**Fourthly**, they all assert, following in the footsteps of *Menno*, that the *Human Nature of Christ*, at the first moment of the **Incarnation** <term>Menſchwordinge: literally "becoming human," the theological concept of the Word taking on human flesh</term>, in the body of the Holy Virgin, was created by GOD out of nothing; but that it subsequently obtained its growth from the blood of that Blessed Mother-Virgin. Yet they never declare themselves on this matter without simultaneously adding a warning that they by no means take part in the Error of the **Valentinians** <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who was accused of denying Christ's true humanity by claiming his body was purely celestial and only passed through Mary "like water through a pipe."</note>, who of old alleged as if Christ had brought His Human Nature with Him from Heaven, and that it had passed through the body of the Blessed Virgin no differently than water through a gutter, without taking anything from the flesh or seed of that Woman. And it is entirely certain that the former opinion is widely and vastly different, and consequently much more tolerable, than the latter: all the more so as it was brought forth from entirely different perspectives. *Menno Simons*, namely, came to this proposition of his because he could not see how the **Humanity** of the Redeemer could be pronounced free from all sinfulness if one believed that it sprouted from Mary; whereas the Valentinians drew their Error from an entirely different and troubled source. The Old Flemings hold this Doctrine of theirs in very high regard and believe that they have a significant advantage because they alone recognize this supposed Truth. The proofs, which I take from their public Sermons, are nearly—

approximately as follows: Christ is placed, as the **Second Adam**, in opposition to the **First Forefather** of Mankind, not in respect to His Divine, but in regard to His Human Nature: but the **Holy Scripture** says, in the contrast between the First and Second Adam, that the latter was from Heaven, and the former was from the Earth. <margin>9. On the Use of Weapons and Resistance.]</margin>
Ninthly, they are very conscientious regarding *Violent Resistance* and the *Use of Weapons*. A large number of Mennonites <term>Mennonites: (Dutch: *Doopsgezinden*) a group of Anabaptist Christians named after Menno Simons</term> have become much more moderate in their thoughts regarding this. But the Old Flemings still desire to be *Defenseless Christians* <note>original: *Weerelooze Christenen*</note> at present; that is to say, they believe that a Christian may never resist unjust Violence, but that he must leave his Goods, Freedom, and Life to his enemies when he is attacked. For this reason, no Member of their Congregation is permitted to carry any Weapon; and their Merchants may never load their Goods into Ships that are armed with heavy artillery. They therefore trade mostly in the Baltic and North Seas, and not in places where one must defend oneself, or where there is danger of falling into the hands of Pirates. In the meantime, their Vessels may indeed undertake the voyage under *Convoy* or Escort of Warships; just as they consider it permissible to live themselves in cities that are fortified with a garrison of Soldiers, Fortifications, and a supply of War Weapons.

And this is that Notorious Proposition for the sake of which the Mennonites <term>Mennonites: Often called "Doopsgezinden" in Dutch; a group of Anabaptist Christian communities tracing their roots to the Radical Reformation</term> were already divided in the time of *Menno Simons* <note>Menno Simons (1496–1561) was the primary leader from whom the Mennonites take their name</note>: for those who were afterwards called *Waterlanders* <term>Waterlanders: A more moderate branch of the Mennonite church, named after the region in North Holland where they originated</term> claimed that a three-fold Warning must always precede any cutting off from the Congregation. *Menno Simons* was at first on the side of these latter mentioned, and only became so strict in this matter toward the end of his life. This the *Old Flemings* concede, but they argue against it that it happened with him as it did with other *Restorers of the Truth*, who only recognized the full brilliance of that *Light* <note>A common metaphor in Reformation writing for divine truth or scriptural clarity</note> over time and by degrees. Meanwhile, it is certain that they do not apply this severity to all cases, but consider a Brotherly Observation or Reproof—in the Manner prescribed by Christ in *Matthew* chapter eighteen <note>Referring to Matthew 18:15-17, which outlines a step-by-step process for resolving conflicts and addressing sin within the church</note>—to be proper, fair, and necessary in some circumstances. Twelfthly, I note regarding the doctrine of *Marriage*, among a portion of these people, the peculiarity which I have already touched upon before: namely, the Dantzigers and all other congregations of the Fine <note>original: "Fyne," a term used for the "pure" or strictest factions of the Mennonite tradition who adhered to rigorous social and religious codes</note> Mennonites, except only the Groningers, do not allow a member of their society to marry *a spouse of another denomination*, even if the one taken in marriage were a person belonging to the "Fine" groups. 14. Concerning 
the Church.
</margin>
*Fourteenthly*: when one considers the first origin of the Mennonite separation from other Christians (†) and reads their oldest writings, one finds that they believed, regarding the Church, that it should consist solely of Saints and Children of God. But since then, they have been convinced otherwise by daily experience. For this reason, they first posit an *Invisible Church*, to which they also count the true Believers from other denominations. And then they also believe in a *Visible True Church* of Christ: but they do not place the marks of the same in the Holiness of Life of all its members; they admit that, in the Visible Church, there are and always will be *Vessels for Honor and Vessels for Dishonor* <note>A biblical reference to 2 Timothy 2:20, acknowledging that any earthly congregation contains both the virtuous and the flawed</note>, good and bad fish. On that account, they place the mark of the True Visible Church in the Truth and Purity of the Doctrine, as well as in the Unity of the members regarding the recognition and acceptance of that Doctrine. They believe that this Pure Truth flourishes in their Church: yet they never speak of this without adding that they wish to leave those who are outside of their circle unjudged, and that it may be enough for them when they find Truth and Unity in their own Congregation, and can call out to one another: *Blessed are you, O Israel! your GOD has revealed Himself to you.* <note>original: "Zalig zyt gy ô Israël! uwe GOD heeft zich aen u geopenbaert." A paraphrase of Deuteronomy 33:29, emphasizing their sense of being a chosen, covenanted community.</note>

It is certain that a Member, while standing under the Ecclesiastical Admonition in this manner, and from whom the fruits and signs of an Improvement are first expected, would not be admitted to the **Lord’s Supper**, in case such were held in the meantime, and such a Member did not indeed make promises, and apply himself as much as possible, to settle himself according to the discretion and satisfaction of the Brethren: but such a Case, or the so-called Small Church Ban (*), is not quite possible. For if we, for example, suppose that someone had taken his legal case before the **Secular Authority** <note>Mennonites traditionally forbade taking fellow believers to court, preferring internal mediation.</note>, and such came to the ear of a Brother, then the matter would be handled shortly. He would either have to decide to withdraw his legal action, or one would proceed to the *Full Ban*. What particularly concerns the *Groningers* <note>A subgroup of the Old Flemish Mennonites known for being exceptionally strict and emphasizing total communal harmony.</note>; with them, the Denial or Suspending of the Holy Lord’s Supper, while retaining the right of Brotherhood, is an absolutely impossible and contradictory matter. For they never hold the Supper except when all the Members of the Congregation collectively stand in a perfectly good trust toward each other; as I thereof, when I to
->their<-

(*) By which someone, not cut off from the Congregation, but is suspended in the Use of the Holy Lord’s Supper.

### S E C T I O N   I I I.

->*On the Church Government of the Old Flemish.*<-

<margin>III. On the CHURCH GOVERNMENT of the Old Flemish.</margin>
The **ECCLESIASTICAL GOVERNMENT** of these congregations rests upon its members of the **Male Sex**. They do not grant the leaders of the Church—or as they call them, the ***Ministers*** <note>original: "Dienaers"; literally "Servants," emphasizing their role as facilitators rather than masters of the faith.</note>—as much power and authority as is common elsewhere. Their members who have a seat and a voice in the **Church Council** <note>original: "Kerkenraed"; the governing body of a local congregation.</note> are the **Elders** or **Bishops**, along with the remaining **Teachers**, and the **Deacons**. In congregations where there are no Elders, the latter two types of ministers alone constitute a legal Church Council.

The Church Council must bring everything of any importance before the general **Brotherhood** <note>The "Broederschap" refers to the collective body of baptized male members who held voting rights in the congregation's affairs.</note>. For example: whenever someone is to be excluded from the ecclesiastical society or readmitted into it; also when someone is to be admitted to **Baptism**, and thus become a member of the congregation for the first time; furthermore, when **Elders**, **Preachers**, and **Deacons**, or **Deaconesses** <note>The mention of Deaconesses is significant, as it shows a specific, formal role for women in social care, even if they were excluded from the primary governing "Brotherhood."</note> are to be chosen; when matters regarding the care and supervision of **Church Property** and the **Poor** must be handled; and so forth. In all such cases, the matter at hand is presented *to the Brotherhood* and given for consideration. Thereupon, one Brother after another—and thus each individually according to his own judgment—is asked by the Ministers in the Church; or at least it is heard from him whether he has anything against the...

They know nothing of **catechisms** <term>Katechisatiën: formal sessions of religious instruction through questions and answers</term>, or public teachings on the doctrine of faith. Hitherto they have had neither public and printed **Confessions of Faith** <term>Geloofsbekentenissen</term> nor **Catechetical Books** <term>Vraagboeken: literally 'question-books' used to teach doctrine</term> in which the specific teachings of their congregations, as they differ from others, are contained. <margin>3. Concerning the Celebration of the Holy Lord’s Supper.</margin>
In the Solemn Celebration of the Holy Lord’s Supper <term>Avondmaels</term>, I have observed the following Circumstances. About four or six weeks beforehand, the Congregation is requested, after the end of the Sermon <term>Predikatie</term>, to remain in the Church; and the Members are asked whether anyone among them has any objection to the Lord's Supper being held at the upcoming usual time. Silence is taken to mean that no one has anything to bring against it. Then, *Self-examination* <note>original: "Zelfsbeproeving"</note> is recommended to everyone. On the appointed Sunday itself, the Service begins with Singing. As soon as that is done, each person prays to themselves in silence; but without kneeling. ...namely, how the Groningers <note>The "Groningers" were a strict branch of the Old Flemish Mennonites, known for their rigorous adherence to tradition and discipline.</note> proceed with this, as they practice this ceremony in some congregations before, and in others after, the use of the Holy Supper <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>The Mennonite term for Communion or the Eucharist.</note> openly in the gathering. In those places where it happens before the enjoyment of the Supper, they do this at the beginning of the service, before the Elders and Teachers enter the church. But usually, they proceed to it only after the Supper is finished: at which time the Elder begins with a speech about this matter; whereupon the congregation, according to custom, says their prayer in silence. Then they begin from the top: the second person washes the feet of the one seated first, after he has pulled off his shoes and stockings, and dries them again with a cloth; after which he kisses him. Upon this, he sits down again and lets himself be treated in the same way by the third person: and in this manner, the ceremony proceeds down the row. The women likewise show each other this service of love in their own order, just as they are seated. The proceedings are concluded by the Elder with an exhortation to humility, love, and harmony.

To him who is chosen as Elder <term>Oudſte</term>, that is, as *Bishop* <term>Biſſchop</term>, this is made known, and the Congregation gives him time for reflection, to be able to consider whether he has the required qualifications for such a Weighty Office. When he sees his way through this, he makes it known to the Brotherhood <term>Broederſchap</term> after some time. Then another Elder is requested, who delivers a Sermon on a Text particularly suited to the occasion, and after finishing it, blesses <note>original: "inzegent". This refers to the formal act of consecration or ordination into the office.</note> the newly elected one. Specifically, the latter kneels down, the other lays both hands on his head, and wishes him all the necessary Gifts of the Holy Spirit, etc. He does this after having first explained to the Congregation the weight of the matter at hand, and having exhorted them to prayer for the Divine Blessing upon it: whereupon the Congregation, according to custom, prays in silence; and subsequently, the Blessing takes place.

6. Concerning the Blessing of the Marriage.

Those persons who wish to join themselves in the Matrimonial State <term>Huwelyken Staet</term> make this known beforehand to the Teacher <term>Leeraer</term> <note>In the Mennonite tradition, a "Teacher" is a recognized minister or preacher authorized to lead the congregation.</note>; and he, after the conclusion of the Service <term>Godsdienst</term>, informs the Congregation of their intention, without any banns <term>Afroeping</term> <note>original: "Afroeping". He exhorts the Congregation to pray to GOD, that He may bless the forthcoming ceremony and be pleased to pour out His Grace upon these persons who intend to enter the Matrimonial State, etc. Thereupon, prayer is offered in silence in the customary manner. This being done, both persons step forward before the Congregation. The Teacher (for it is not necessary that this be done by a Bishop <term>Bisschop</term> <note>Referring to the "Elder" or "Oudste," the highest rank of ministry mentioned on the previous page.</note>) asks them, *whether it is still their will to join together in Wedlock?* and they answer that with *Yes*. He sets before them the duties of married folk using the words of Holy Scripture, and asks them, *whether they wish to keep these Commandments of Marriage according to this Precept?* They promise this and give each other their hand. The Teacher takes their hands in his right hand and blesses them. Then those persons go to the City Hall or Town House and likewise have themselves joined in Matrimony by the Magistrates <term>Schepenen</term> <note>original: "Schepenen". These were local judicial and administrative officers in the Netherlands, similar to aldermen, who handled civil marriage requirements.</note>.

And for that reason, a Reformed Christian has entered into a complete and, according to all required circumstances, legal marriage as soon as it has been confirmed by the Reformed Minister through the blessing <term>Inzegening</term> <note>The formal religious consecration of the marriage.</note>; and he never goes to the Council or Town Hall to obtain secular legality for himself. So too, when other fellow believers allow themselves to be blessed in the Reformed Church, they are bound with the full consequence of indissolubility, of inheritance rights, and whatever else there may be, and they do not first seek these rights through a so-called *Copulatie* <note>original: "Copulatie", a Latin term for the formal joining or binding together in marriage.</note> or union at the Town Hall. All other denominations, both of Christians and of Jews, are considered in these lands to be tolerated; and their ecclesiastical acts, church books, and teachers have no secular or civil legality. Consequently, they cannot, through the blessing that occurs among them, establish such a marriage that has the secular and civil-legal consequences and effects of a Public Matrimonial Bond (*). In short, if complaints were to arise and disputes were to break out, the Authorities would regard that marriage transaction as something that is void and powerless in civil matters, and has no legality <margin>* Has no legal standing <note>original German/Latin: "Keinen Fidem hat."</note></margin>*. Therefore, all those persons who wish to enter into marriage must seek a secular or civil legality for their marriage at the Town Hall. And in this, this order is maintained: they must first present themselves and have themselves recorded in the Marriage Register <term>Trouwboek</term> at the City or Town Hall. <margin>9. Of the Sermon Texts.</margin>
All sermon texts are free and depend upon the Teacher’s <term>Teacher: original *Leeraer*, the term for a Mennonite minister</term> own choice. They also maintain the custom of not basing their *Confessional Sermons* <note>Sermons where the articles of faith are explained to new members</note> on a specific Scripture text. And truly, a sermon in which a Scripture text is explained is not so much a sermon as it is an *Explanatory and Applied Treatise* (*), delivered either from memory or from a written manuscript. It appears that the use of texts was introduced as an aid for those who were not capable enough to compose a long and coherent oration from their own internal resources.

<margin>10. Of the Customs regarding the Ban.</margin>
The customs regarding the *Church Ban* <term>The Ban: original *den Ban*, the practice of excommunication or formal shunning used to maintain the purity of the church</term> are as follows: When a fellow member of the Congregation has sinned, and the Church Council <term>Church Council: original *Kerkenraed*, the governing body of elders and deacons</term> has gained knowledge of it—whether through common rumor or through a Brother or Sister—the accused is called into the consistory room and is questioned and examined there. He either confesses his transgression or denies it; in the latter case, he must be convicted by reasonable evidence or the testimony of two witnesses. Whether or not this occurs, he is either brought before the Brothers <note>The "Brothers" refers to the male members of the congregation who held voting power in church matters</note>, and his transgression is laid open to them with the necessary circumstances and evidence (at which time he is free to bring forward whatever he deems best for his defense), or he departs, as commonly happens, not wishing to be a witness to the accusation that will be made against him. ...dogs, and will not throw pearls before swine. <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6, used here to justify excluding excommunicated members from hearing the Word of God.</note> The other Congregations of the *Refined* <note>original: *Fynen*, a term for the stricter, more traditionalist branches of the Mennonites</note>, on the contrary, gladly allow the excommunicated person to enter the Church; because the Apostle has commanded that such sinners should not be regarded as enemies, but exhorted as brothers. Indeed, they even require of him that, while under the Ban, he diligently attends the religious services, as a sign of his repentance and improvement.

<margin>
II. Regarding the Custom for the Readmission of an Excommunicated Person.
</margin>
Now, when the sinner wishes to be *re-accepted and admitted* <note>original: *Op- en Aengenomen*</note> into the Congregation once more, he must request one or another Brother to closely observe his conduct and the fruits of his repentance, so that they may have the opportunity and reason to provide a good testimony of his improvement to the Congregation. Then he seeks to convince these Brothers of his sincere repentance, and subsequently requests that they report his desire to be Readmitted to the Teachers <term>Teacher: original *Leeraer*, the term for a Mennonite minister</term> and the Congregation, and to recommend him as best as possible; especially, that they request the Teachers to be so kind as to call the Brotherhood together concerning this matter. This is done; and the Teachers open their opinion to the Congregation, stating whether they view the sinner's repentance as sincere and sufficient, or whether they believe that the Readmission ought to be postponed a while longer. When the Teachers judge from the signs of repentance that the sinner is fit to receive the Forgiveness of Sins, and have declared this to the Brotherhood, then each Brother is individually asked whether he still finds anything scandalous or offensive in the fallen one? And in the event that they have nothing to object, then...

CHURCH CUSTOMS OF THE OLD FLEMISH.

...the sinner <note>original: *Zondaer*</note> either appears immediately himself, or he is already present during the proceedings.

The Elder or a Teacher <term>Teacher: original *Leeraer*, the traditional Mennonite term for a minister or pastor</term> then places his conduct up to this point before his eyes, and asks him whether he acknowledges that he has been punished fairly and justly, according to the precept of the Divine Word? In response to this, he must fall upon his knees in the presence of the Brotherhood; and then the Grace is held before him, which GOD has granted him in this matter, by bestowing upon him a yearning for Repentance; he is exhorted to a true contrition of heart; and the Brotherhood is requested to offer a prayer for him; which is performed in the usual silence <note>Mennonite tradition often favored silent prayer over spoken liturgy, believing it allowed for more sincere individual communion with God</note>. When this has occurred, the Penitent Sinner is addressed again; and he is comforted and strengthened with the hope that GOD has forgiven him his sin, and has cast them into the depths of the sea <note>A reference to Micah 7:19: "You will again have compassion on us; you will tread our sins underfoot and hurl all our iniquities into the depths of the sea."</note>. Thereupon the Teacher gives him his hand, raises him from the earth, and receives him as a Newly-accepted Brother with a kiss <note>Known as the "Holy Kiss" or "Kiss of Peace," a biblical practice (Romans 16:16) used to signify full reconciliation and fellowship</note>. The same takes place in the event that the excommunicated person is a female. Finally, all the Brothers are requested to forgive the Re-admitted Person for the sin and offense, just as GOD has forgiven them; and to recognize him or her as a Brother or Sister, and never to unkindly cast up the previous failing.

### V. PART. OF THE MENNONITES.

->PART V.<-

->On the Outward State of these Congregations.<-

<margin>
V. Concerning the EXTERNAL STATE of the Old Flemish Congregations.
</margin>
<margin>
1. Concerning their Church Buildings and Institutions.
</margin>
THE church buildings of the Old Flemish <term>Old Flemish: a conservative branch of the Mennonites known for strict adherence to tradition</term> possess no outward grandeur; just as the meeting places of the dissenting denominations in the Netherlands are generally built in such a way that they cannot easily be recognized as churches from the outside. <note>This refers to the Dutch tradition of "schuilkerken" or hidden churches; while non-Reformed groups were tolerated, their houses of worship often had to look like ordinary houses or warehouses from the street.</note> However, one must except from this the churches of the Established Religion <note>The Dutch Reformed Church, the state-supported church of the era</note>, as well as those of the Lutheran community and the synagogues of both the Portuguese and High German Jews in Amsterdam; as these clearly enough display the external appearance of churches. The meeting places of the Old Flemish are, regarding their size, proportioned to the number of their members. In Amsterdam, the church of the so-called *Dantzigers* <note>A specific subgroup of Old Flemish Mennonites with historical ties to the city of Danzig</note> (for other varieties of Old Flemish are not found in that city) stands on the canal called the *Agterburgwal* (*) near the *Lynbaensteeg*; where a sign hangs depicting several jugs; for which reason, for the sake of brevity, it is customary to say that they hold their meeting *at* or *in the Little Jugs* <note>original: *in de Kruikjes*</note>. I explicitly mention the location where this church stands, as I shall also do for the following ones, so that a stranger in this sprawling city might more easily inquire after these churches; since they are not even known to all the inhabitants. This congregation has between sixty and seventy baptized members.

A few years ago in Amsterdam, they also obtained from the High Government the freedom <note>meaning legal permission or exemption</note> which is likewise granted to all other denominations, and which benefits their brethren elsewhere; namely, that their church buildings are exempt from all *Taxes* <note>original: *Lasten*; referring to the various property taxes and municipal duties of the 18th century</note> to which other buildings are subject. If they wished to establish houses for Orphans, the Elderly, and similar buildings, or to apply a portion of their Ecclesiastical Income to the purchase of any houses from which they used the rent and income for the service of the poor, the same would follow; and they would be exempt from paying the usual Taxes on all such Lands that belonged to such a Christian Intention. The Old Flemish <term>Old Flemish: a conservative branch of the Mennonite movement known for strict discipline and simple living</term> claim that they have no great Ecclesiastical Income, but that most needs must be met through regular Alms, or through extraordinary collections. Meanwhile, they do, however, possess some Capital and Property in most places; though they may not be as richly provided for as other Mennonite <note>original: *Doopsgezinde*</note> congregations are. They have no *Orphanages*; but they place their Orphans with Fellow Members of the Congregation to be raised, and provide them with something for this from the Common Alms. Other incapacitated or *Needy Members* are likewise assisted with money.

Since they do not provide their Teachers with any salary, it simply depends on whether a congregation is fortunate enough to find many capable members among them: in such a case, they may appoint as many Teachers as they see fit. This provides some relief in the service to the others, who nevertheless cannot entirely set aside their worldly livelihood for their preaching office. Their Teachers and Bishops are craftsmen, or they engage in trade.

Congregations of the *Old Flemish*, or otherwise *Old Frisians*, are, on account of their unrefined and secluded life, particularly regarding their clothing, counted among the <term>Most Refined</term> <note>original: *Alderfynsten*; the strictest, most conservative branch of the Old Flemish Mennonites who resisted modern influences</note>; and each of them lives for itself, or stands in brotherly union with only one or another. The *Dantzigers* do the same in their turn; and the *Groningers* <note>a subgroup originally from the Groningen area</note> also maintain this footing. Some of these congregations have already fallen into decline since ancient times. For example: in very old times, a schism occurred in Friesland while the Roman religion <note>Catholicism</note> still ruled in these lands, because some brothers—as was required in those days—went with their Roman-minded fellow craftsmen to a burial according to the laws of the <term>Guild-chambers</term> <note>original: *Gildekamers*; professional associations that required members to participate in public religious ceremonies</note> of that time. This involved walking in a procession or solemn parade in which the Cross and other Roman relics were carried at the front. Other brothers held this to be sinful; and because of this, it came to a division. ...for some time, it occurred to some Brothers of the same group to visit the Meeting of the <term>Collegiants</term> <note>A non-dogmatic religious movement in the Netherlands that rejected formal church hierarchy and allowed any member to speak; they often met in Rijnsburg</note>; and one of them went so far as to partake in the Lord's Supper with that Society at Rijnsburg, without in the least suspending his connection to his own Congregation. After he had been excluded in this manner, it was found that his wife ate with him at one and the same table; and she moreover confessed of her own accord that she did not shun him in any way. Consequently, the same fate and judgment befell her. But when, notwithstanding this, some other Brothers again went to the Collegiants and were called before the Brotherhood because of it, one of the accused stood up and delivered a Moving and Fiery Oration concerning the Ban, in which he demonstrated its proper limits and purposes. He framed everything to the best advantage of his own conduct and that of his fellow Brothers, and thus silenced the Congregation. Since that time, this practice—previously judged very harmful—has been <term>overlooked</term> <note>original: *door de vingeren ziet*; literally "seen through the fingers," meaning to intentionally ignore or tolerate a forbidden act</note>. Meanwhile, the right of Brotherhood nevertheless remained open to all *Mennonites* <term>Mennonites</term> <note>original: *Doopsgezinden*; literally "baptism-minded," the standard Dutch term for Mennonites</note> everywhere, among all the Congregations.

<margin>Concerning their New Schism.</margin>
In the beginning, these last-mentioned Churches seemed to be unified in everything, both when viewed as a whole and when observing their individual members. Their Confessions of Faith <term>Confessions of Faith</term> <note>original: *Geloofsbelydeniffen*; formal documents outlining a group's theological stance</note> were open to everyone: and these were—to put it in few words—regarding Doctrine, all in agreement with the views of the *Evangelical-Lutheran* Church, if one excepted these four specific points; namely, *Baptism*, the *Office of the Magistracy*, the *Use of Weapons*, and the *Oath* <note>These four points—believer's baptism, refusal to serve in government or the military, and the refusal to swear oaths—formed the core of the Anabaptist "radical" distinction from other Protestants</note>. However, there was no lack of people in the meantime who began to think differently regarding many of the most important doctrinal points, and who partly fell toward the *Socinian-leaning* <term>Socinians</term> <note>A rationalist sect that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ, emphasizing human reason</note> among the *Remonstrants* <term>Remonstrants</term> <note>A group of Dutch Arminians who favored a more liberal, less strict interpretation of predestination</note>, and partly fell away to the *Socinians* themselves. Yet, this did not immediately come to light openly. One Congregation stood more firmly on the Confessions of Faith than the—

From his writings, it appears that regarding these doctrines he asserted roughly the same as what is taught now—and was already partly taught then—by the *Remonstrants* <term>Remonstrants</term> <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius who favored a more moderate, less rigid view of predestination and grace than the strict Calvinists</note>. Alliances between entire congregations are founded upon that same ground of continuous unanimity in the same doctrine of faith and understanding of confessions. The confessions of the Baptists <term>Doopsgezinden: the standard Dutch term for Mennonites, literally 'baptism-minded'</term> are essentially the same, yet they are of four types: namely, the *Waterlander Confession*; the *Frisian Confession*; the *High German Confessions*; and the *Flemish Confessions*.

1. The *Waterlander Confession* was already drawn up in the year 1581; we shall speak of it in a subsequent note.

2. The *Frisian Confession* is not actually a confession drawn up in the presence of or at the request of that congregation; but was first placed by *Pieter Jansz. Twisk* and his assistants (though with the knowledge and prior approval of *various godly persons practiced in the Word of Truth*) in the year 1617 for the *History of the True Witnesses of Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Historie der waerachtige Getuigen Jesu Christi"</note>, published in quarto at Hoorn by *Zacharias Cornelisz.*; and afterwards, revised by the same authors, printed in octavo by the aforementioned bookseller in 1620.

3. There are two *High German Confessions*: *firstly*, the *Concept of Cologne*, drawn up as a foundation for the union struck at Cologne between the High German Baptists and some of the Frisians in the year 1591; *secondly*, the so-called *Jan Centsen’s Confession*, otherwise known as the *High German* or *German Confession*, first delivered orally and thereafter, at the request of the Flemish, in writing in the year 1630 by commissioners of these United High German and Frisian congregations to the Flemish.

4. Finally, there are the *Flemish Confessions*: *Firstly*, the *Confession* of 1626 drawn up by *Jaques Outerman*, otherwise of *Rennegom*, Teacher and Elder at Haarlem, signed by him and twenty of his fellow teachers from other cities, and subsequently submitted to the Court of Holland, containing only their views regarding the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of the Incarnation of the Son of God. *Secondly*, the *Olive Branch* <note>original: "Olyftakje"</note>, or the Peace Presentation and Confession, sent in writing everywhere among their people by the Flemish congregation of Amsterdam in 1627, approved, and published in print in 1629. *Thirdly*, the *Confession of Adriaen Cornelisz.* drawn up at Dordrecht in the year 1632, and laid as a foundation for the union then struck there between most of the Flemish congregations, which in many places...

# I. PART. THE MENNONITES.

<margin>DOCTRINE OF THE WATERLANDER FLEMISH.</margin>
Congregations require of all those who wish to enjoy the Holy Supper <note>The Lord's Supper or Holy Communion.</note> among them, that they first be properly baptized—that is, in their adult years—and secondly, that they accept the Confession of Faith of their Church. Consequently, they would not admit any Protestant, nor even a fellow Mennonite <note>original: "Doopsgezinde"</note> who openly deviates from them in the Doctrine of the Holy Trinity, or of Justification <note>A central theological concept concerning how a person is made right with God.</note>, and the like, to the Supper (*). It is true that here and there they have some Teachers who are somewhat more flexible in these matters, or who seek to manage with moderate Forms of Requirement <note>Formal statements or conditions used to determine eligibility for church membership or communion.</note>, particularly regarding members of other Churches who were baptized in their infancy; however, they must nonetheless admit that the greatest part of their Church still stands firm on this point. For the mutual enjoyment of the Holy Supper, **Adult Baptism** is almost a more essential requirement among them than complete agreement in Doctrine. This is evident as they must currently tolerate members at the Lord’s Table who, for example, also associate with the Collegiants <note>A 17th and 18th-century Dutch religious movement that valued individual spiritual freedom and did not require adherence to strict creeds; they often met in "colleges" or study groups.</note>, despite having reason to believe that these individuals harbor many deviating opinions; whereas no Lutheran or Reformed person would be admitted by them without **Rebaptism** <note>original: "Wederdoop." This highlights the strictness of the group: they prioritized the physical act of adult baptism over doctrinal purity in some cases, but refused to recognize infant baptism as valid under any circumstance.</note>. Quite different is the position of the Mennonites on the Remonstrant-leaning <note>Remonstrants followed the teachings of Jacobus Arminius, favoring a more liberal and inclusive approach to theology compared to the strict Calvinism of the Reformed Church.</note> side: as they make no difficulty in asserting that for anyone who takes God’s Word as their *Guideline* and walks blamelessly, the Lord’s Table ought to be open. In the first sense, it can be enjoyed by those who were only baptized in their infancy. As contradictory and strange as that expression—receiving the Lord's Supper *as a Guest*, or *guest-wise*, and not as a Brother—may seem (given that this Meal ought to be a Seal and Monument of the closest Brotherly Love and Union), it is, on the contrary, quite clear and understandable in the eyes of this Congregation. For the Lord's Supper, in their opinion, is simply what it is according to the modern conceptions of many Episcopal Teachers <note>Referring to clergy of the Church of England (Anglicans).</note> in England; namely, solely and only a Ceremony or Solemnity by which one represents to oneself the Death of Christ. Could not all those who believe that JESUS is the Son of God, and died for the salvation of mankind, achieve these objectives simultaneously without being bound to one another?

...as Aldermen; however, when punishments or capital cases <note>original: "halszaeken," literally "neck-matters," referring to crimes punishable by death.</note> are to be judged, they withdraw. Meanwhile, it remains a firm principle among the first two of these three congregations—namely, the *Frisians* and the *Mennonite Waterlanders*—that they cannot hold any significant public office <term>Overheitsampt|A high-ranking position in the magistracy or government</term> with a clear conscience. This is not because they consider the office itself to be unlawful or unbefitting of a Christian, but rather because the role requires one—according to the present state of affairs—to swear oaths and require others to swear them, as well as to promote military matters and perform other duties they deem improper.

In contrast, regarding those *Waterlanders* who lean toward the Remonstrant <note>A more liberal branch of Dutch Protestantism that favored human free will over strict predestination.</note> side, it appears they are not only beginning to drift from this cautious doctrine, but would also—if the laws of these lands permitted—willingly demonstrate in practice that they are not so strict in their views. They make little difficulty in admitting that a considerable number of their brothers have, in this regard, adopted the general views of the major Christian Churches. Nevertheless, this shift cannot easily manifest in practice, because all significant public offices must be held by members of the Reformed Church <note>The state-sanctioned Calvinist church of the Dutch Republic, which held a monopoly on political office.</note>. It is enough, for the time being, that their congregation no longer demands that a member think exactly as other Anabaptists used to regarding this and other matters.

<margin>
9. On Violent Resistance.
</margin>
Ninth: Formerly, all Anabaptists <note>original: "Doopsgezinden," the Dutch term for Mennonites</note> held the view that a Christian must absolutely endure all injustice and in no way repel Violence with Violence; for which reason they held the *Use of Arms* to be entirely forbidden for them. All their Confessions of Faith convey this; and the Old Flemish are still in favor of this Thesis. But the Anabaptists of the three Congregations of which I am currently speaking deviated significantly from this: they no longer wish to be called *Defenseless* <term>Weerelooze|Historically, Mennonites used this term to define themselves as non-resistant, refusing to carry weapons or serve in the military</term> Christians, as their ancestors called themselves; but they are, as they say, *Revenge-less* <term>Wrackelooze|A theological distinction where self-defense is permitted, but seeking vengeance or initiating conflict is forbidden</term> Christians—that is, those who practice no revenge or violence to attack others. They consider it permissible to repel unlawful Violence with Counter-violence. For that reason, they make no objection to placing their Goods on Armed Vessels <note>Referring to merchant ships equipped with cannons for defense against pirates or enemy nations.</note>.

Some, who do not understand the ancient languages <note>Referring to Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, which were standard for university-trained theologians.</note>, were made capable of and accustomed to public speaking in their youth within the meetings of the <term>Collegianten</term> <note>A non-sectarian religious movement that held "colleges" or meetings where any member could speak; they heavily influenced the more liberal Mennonites.</note>; or they acquired this skill through the Exercises which these Mennonites establish here and there in their Churches, and of which I shall speak in the following pages. Still others have received some degree of instruction from Lutheran or Reformed Preachers.

<margin>CHURCH GOVERNANCE OF THE WATERLANDERS, FLEMISH, AND FRISIANS. 7. Regarding the Subsidies for the Studying Youth.</margin>
This same Congregation provides a yearly financial subsidy to a fair number of students, so that they may pursue their studies <note>original: "Wetenschappen" - referring here to academic disciplines or "sciences" in the broad 18th-century sense</note> with more success. They do not readily disclose how high the number of these young men is; however, it is known that each of them receives two hundred and fifty Dutch Guilders annually. They currently place great emphasis on philosophy; especially on the doctrine of **Natural Law** <term>Natuurlyk Recht</term>: for they hope that they can significantly strengthen their arguments for **Tolerance** <term>Verdraegzaemheit</term> from it. From among these students, the other congregations in the Netherlands often choose their **Ministers** (*) <note>original: "Leeraers" - literally "Teachers," the term used by Mennonites for their clergy</note>; just as I shall say more on this matter in what follows.

nonetheless, in their principal **Congregations** <note>original: "Gemeenten"</note>, one rarely finds a **Teacher** <note>original: "Leeraer" — a common Mennonite term for a minister or preacher</note> who cannot be counted to some extent among the learned, and who does not at least understand Latin or some other languages. Their Teachers are commonly merchants, apothecaries, etc., and often also **Doctors of Medicine**. However, I also find among them men who have devoted themselves properly and solely to the **Sciences** <note>the term "Wetenschappen" here refers broadly to academic scholarship, including humanities and theology</note>, and follow no other trade. Such a class of men is, however, found much more abundantly among the **Remonstrant-leaning** <note>liberal Mennonites who shared theological views with the Arminians</note> Congregations. The **Orthodox** <note>original: "Regtzinnige" — the more traditionalist branch of the Mennonites</note> always have certain Teachers who possess both the gift and ability to bring young people so far in the necessary Sciences, especially in **Theology** <term>Godgeleerdheit</term>, that they can undertake the office of Teacher. For example, in the Mennonite Waterlander and Flemish Congregation in Amsterdam, this was done in former times by the well-known **Hermannus Schyn**, who was at once a Doctor of Medicine and a Preacher in this Congregation. Currently, their studying youth hold themselves to Mr. **Gerardus Maetschoen**, a Teacher who at the same time understands the art of the apothecary and practices it in his own measure alongside the service of his Office. It is this man who intends to bring to light an *Extensive History of the Mennonites* (*). For the rest, the young men—

### III. PART. OF THE ANABAPTISTS.

<margin>
CHURCH GOVERNMENT OF THE WATERLANDERS, FLEMISH, AND FRISIANS.

...those who wish to apply themselves to the **Sciences** <term>Wetenschappen — here referring to academic scholarship and higher learning</term> also, when they see fit, attend the **Universities** <note>original: "Hooge Scholen"</note>. The aforementioned Congregation likewise provides annual maintenance for a certain number of young men. However, they would not like to see these students go to the Remonstrant professors, or to the previously mentioned Anabaptist professor. They fear that they might adopt the stances of these men; and those cannot be approved in the Congregations of which I now speak.

<margin>
9. Concerning the Salary or Remuneration of the Teachers.
</margin>
I have already stated that the *Frisian* Teachers <note>original: "Leeraers" — the term used for Mennonite ministers</note> usually serve without remuneration. In contrast, the Teachers among the *Mennonite* Waterlanders have an income; though it is modest. In Amsterdam, each Teacher has Twelve hundred Dutch **Guilders** <term>Guldens — the standard currency of the Netherlands at the time</term>. But the **Remonstrant-leaning** <note>liberal Mennonites who aligned with the Arminians</note> congregation gives each of them Two thousand (*) such Guilders. Outside that city, the Teachers on both the Waterlander and Flemish sides have an annual salary of Four hundred to Six hundred Guilders, according to what the capacity of their individual Congregations allows; and in prominent Congregations, even more (†). Both these groups still have some Teachers here and there in the countryside who until now serve without pay, and consequently are simply the best and most capable members of such a Congregation; who otherwise manage their worldly affairs. Thus, they also frequently have such men who possess no "proper scholarship" so-called, but concern themselves only with the books which in the **Dutch language** <note>original: "Nederduitsche Tael"</note>...

---

(*) Eighteen hundred Guilders.
(†) There are several Congregations among these where the salary amounts to between Six hundred and One thousand Guilders.
