### IV. PART.

->*Of the Religious Exercises and Ecclesiastical Customs of the Frisians, Waterlanders, and Flemish.*<-

<margin>
IV. Of their RELIGIOUS EXERCISES AND ECCLESIASTICAL CUSTOMS.
</margin>
In their CHURCH CUSTOMS and RELIGIOUS EXERCISES, as well as in all other matters that can be brought under that heading, these Three Congregations of the **Anabaptists** <term>Doopsgezinden — literally 'baptism-minded,' the common Dutch term for Mennonites</term> agree reasonably well. In the principal cities, the **Ministers** <term>Predikanten — a term for ordained clergy</term> dress in the same manner as the Reformed and Lutheran teachers of these lands: namely, they go with **Cloak and Bands** <note>original: "Mantel en Bef" — the formal clerical attire consisting of a long black robe and the distinctive white neck tabs</note>, as is the custom in this country. In common social interaction, they are also given the same titles of honor as the others. The congregation calls them ***Domines*** <note>original: "Domine's" — the standard Dutch title for a minister, derived from the Latin for 'Lord' or 'Master'</note>, just as the ministers of other churches are called. <margin>IV. On their RELIGIOUS EXERCISES and ECCLESIASTICAL CUSTOMS.</margin>
In their CHURCH CUSTOMS and RELIGIOUS EXERCISES, as well as in all other things that can be brought thereto, these Three Congregations of the **Anabaptists** <term>Doopsgezinden — literally "baptism-minded," the standard Dutch term for Mennonites, who practice adult baptism upon confession of faith</term> agree reasonably well. On Sunday morning, a sermon is delivered which contains nothing other than a confession of faith regarding all the main doctrines of Christianity. When this is concluded and the service has ended, the **Baptismal Candidates** <term>Doopelingen</term> appear before the Teachers and Deacons in the **Consistory Room** <term>Kerkenkamer — the room where the church leadership meets</term>, and each brings two **Witnesses** with them. One of the Ministers speaks: he places before the candidates the gravity of their intention; and he exhorts them in a moving manner that they should know their sins, become poor in spirit, take refuge in the **wounds of Christ** <note>original: "wonden van Christus" — a common 18th-century expression emphasizing the redemptive power of Christ’s suffering</note> and His Grace, and prepare themselves with all earnestness. The Ministers have significantly more freedom in this regard than among other denominations. In some Congregations, the Teacher kneels down by the Table; in others, he offers this prayer standing. <margin>
*And the ministers and deacons carry the bread and the cup around.* <note>original German: "Und die Prediger und Diakonen tragen das Brod und den Kelk herum."</note>

The *Distribution* proceeds in various ways. In the *Flemish* and *Frisian* Congregations, from of old, the Members of the Congregation remain seated, and the Ministers go through the Church and give the Bread to each in their place, while the Deacons bring them the Cup in the same manner *. In the *Waterland* Congregations, the Participants come to the Table. In the United Congregations, where the Members on either side were not otherwise satisfied in this regard, it is done one time in this manner, and another time in that manner. The first-mentioned manner is followed, for example, in the Congregation of the *Sun* in Amsterdam, notwithstanding that they also have Waterlanders among them: and since the Congregation, which I call the *Remonstrant-minded* <note>The Remonstrants were a liberal theological movement; some Mennonite congregations adopted their more open views on church membership and doctrine</note> (though not all its Members are strictly adherents to the Remonstrant positions), has two Churches, they also act in that manner in the Church at the *Lamb*; on the contrary, in the Church at the *Tower*, the Brothers and Sisters go to the Table. In Rotterdam, both these manners are observed alternately; this Congregation furthermore being in union with the <term>Mennonite-minded <note>original: "Mennonitiefchgezinde"</note></term> Congregation of the Waterlanders and Flemish in Amsterdam (*). All the Frisian Congregations adhere to the first-

...the aforementioned manner. I shall first describe that method.

Namely, the Minister <note>original: "Predikant"</note> breaks a small piece of the Bread which he holds in his hand, and gives such a piece to each of his Co-ministers <note>original: "Medeleeraers," literally "fellow-teachers," a common term for Mennonite clergy</note> and to the Deacons, and says:

> "Receive, dear Brother, the Bread of the Holy Supper; take it, eat it, and remember thereby the bitter Suffering and Dying of JESUS, and that his Body was broken on the tree <note>original: "stam," meaning the trunk or stem</note> of the Cross."

Thereupon the other Ministers step down from their places and divide themselves, each to one side of the Church: they are each accompanied by a Deacon, who carries one of the small baskets with Bread. They go to each Member of the Church and give him a broken piece of Bread, without saying anything. While this takes place, the Twenty-second Psalm is sung in some Congregations; but in others, a portion of Christ’s Suffering <note>The Passion narrative</note> is read (*): in the Frisian Congregation, at certain times the Suffering of the Savior <note>original: "Zaligmaker"</note> is presented in an expanded manner <note>i.e., a paraphrase or commentary</note>, and not merely with the words of Scripture (†). After the breaking and distribution of the Bread, the Ministers gather again before the Table, and the one officiating the ceremony stands in the middle: and they cease with the Singing, or with the Reading and Speaking. He says:

(†) This is done by the Minister, who then either remains standing before the Table while his fellow brothers perform the Distribution, or speaks continuously during the distribution, as was the custom among the Old Flemish.

Let me now further report how things proceed in the Congregations <note>original: "Gemeenten"</note> where the Members approach the Table of the Lord. Namely, there a full Table sits together; they eat the Bread, and drink from the Cup <note>original: "Drinkbeker"</note>. At the first Table, the Minister <note>original: "Predikant"</note> gives an address and a prayer for both the receiving of the Bread and the receiving of the Wine, in the same manner as I have mentioned before. When the first have finished, they return to their places, and others arrive. These eat and drink without further address or public Prayer: and as soon as they have communed <note>original: "gecommuniceert"</note> they also leave the Table again; and a third portion approaches. This continues until every one of the Members has partaken of the Signs of the Covenant <note>term: "Verbondstekenen," a theological term for the bread and wine representing the New Covenant</note>. Meanwhile, the Twenty-third Psalm is likewise sung (*). The Table is generally so long that fourteen or fifteen persons can find a place at it.

---

> (*) This is at least not in use everywhere; especially not in Congregations that are somewhat numerous. But it proceeds there in this manner. First come the Teachers <note>original: "Leeraers"</note> and Deacons, both those in Service and those Resting <note>term: "Resting" (Rustende) refers to retired or emeritus office-bearers who are no longer in active service</note>; then the Brothers; subsequently the Sisters. When the First Table is seated, the Blessing and Prayer are performed, just as in the other custom. Then the Teacher distributes the Bread and begins the Presentation of the History of the Passion of Christ, adding applicable Remarks. When they have eaten, he distributes the Cup and continues further until they have drunk, and closes with a Benediction. He continues in this way at the second, and each of the following Tables, until everything is done. He makes his Remarks shorter or longer, depending on the number of table-guests <note>original: "Dischgenooten"</note> present; so that he may present the entire Passion narrative.

When everything has been completed, whether in this latter way or in the first-mentioned manner, the Teacher <note>original: "Leeraer," the term used by Mennonites for their ministers</note> goes back up to the pulpit and offers Thanksgiving and Prayers; and the service is thus concluded in the usual manner. In the afternoon, or among the Frisians in the evening, a Thanksgiving sermon <note>original: "Dankpredikatie"</note> is given; for which appropriate texts and subjects are chosen. Several Congregations hold the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Avondmael"</note> three times a year; others twice. The Congregation of the United Waterlanders and Flemings, whose members are mostly Remonstrant-minded <term>Remonstrantschgezind: followers of the Arminian theological tradition, known for a more liberal outlook on grace and free will compared to strict Calvinism</term>, holds it five times a year; for it has two churches: and when long ago the Union of the Waterlanders and Flemings took place (*), the custom was preserved in each of those churches as it had been from of old. Most all the Congregations of these three branches <note>original: "Smaldeelen"</note> have fixed times for this Holy Ceremony. For example, the Congregation in Amsterdam, which meets in *the Sun* <note>original: "de Zon," a church named after the image on its gable stone</note>, holds the Lord's Supper on the first Sunday in March, then the first Sunday in July, and finally on the second Sunday in November.

(*) The Union of the Waterlanders, whether with the Flemings, or with the United Flemish, High Germans, and Frisians, did not happen all at once. That of the United Flemish, Frisian, and High German Congregation at *the Lamb* <note>original: "bij het Lam"</note> with the *Waterlander* congregation at *the Tower* <note>original: "bij den Thoren"</note> in Amsterdam, to speak of none earlier, occurred, as we have already noted, on June 1, 1668. That of the Congregation of *the Sun* with the majority of the Waterlanders, etc., of North Holland on July 18, 1674. That of the Waterlanders with the Flemings in Zaendam on February 25, 1700; in Rotterdam on June 6, 1700; and in Leiden on February 13, 1701, to mention no later ones.

### THE PRESENT STATE. Chapter II.

<margin>
CHURCH CUSTOMS OF THE WATERLANDERS etc.
7. Of the Consecration of Church Ministers.
</margin>
When someone is to be accepted, either as a Candidate Minister <term>Proponent: a theological student who has passed their exams and is licensed to preach, but is not yet fully ordained to administer sacraments</term>, or as an ordinary Teacher <note>original: "Leeraer," the traditional Mennonite term for a minister or pastor</note>, it is currently the custom among the *Mennonite-minded* Congregation of the United Flemings and Waterlanders that the Teacher who has instructed him provides testimony of his competence. Then the Candidate is called before several *Delegates* from the Church Council <note>original: "Kerkenraed," the governing body of the local church</note> and is examined or investigated by them. Upon this, he must sign in writing that he intends to hold fast to the Confessions of Faith of the Congregation. With this, he receives the permission and the appointment to preach in the Congregation as a Candidate. When he is then to become an Ordinary Teacher, who may also administer the Sacraments, he is asked in the presence of the Congregation: *Firstly*, whether he intends to persevere steadfastly in the Confessions of Faith of the Congregation (*)? and *secondly*, whether he intends to confirm his Teaching with a Holy Life? After he has testified to this, hands are laid upon him by a Teacher, and a certain *Formula of Consecration* <note>original: "Formulier van Inzegening"</note> is pronounced over him in the presence of the Congregation, which was composed by the Reverend *Hermannus Schyn* <note>Hermannus Schyn (1633–1727) was an influential Mennonite physician and historian in Amsterdam</note> and has since always been used on such occasions. Anyone can easily imagine that this Formula, and the commitment to the Confessions of Faith, has no place in the *Remonstrant-minded* <term>Remonstrantschgezind: influenced by Arminian theology, which favored religious tolerance and a less rigid adherence to specific creeds compared to traditional Calvinism</term> Congregation, and that in

(*) The Reverend Author intended to present these questions not exactly word-for-word, but in substance; however, this Congregation does not understand that the Young Teachers shall accept those Confessions as being of equal authority with God’s Word, but always as subject to *the Word of God*.

(*) During the *Troubles* <note>referring to the Eighty Years' War or the Dutch Revolt against Spain</note>, and for many years thereafter, the wedding was solemnized within the Congregation among all Mennonites, without having it registered by their Magistrates. Before or during the year 1597, several Mennonite couples in Westzaan, Uitgeest, and Abbekerk were prosecuted by the Bailiff of Kennemerland as *Contraveners* <note>original: "Contravenieurs," meaning those who violate or act against a law</note> of the aforementioned Ordinance. A petition was made by Request to be allowed to persist in that custom, but it was rejected by Their Noble Great Mightinesses. Sometime later, those from Westzaan renewed a similar Request with the Delegated Councilors of Holland and West Friesland, declaring that they judged this in good conscience to belong to their exercise of religion; this Request was supported by the Regents of Westzaan. In the year 1606, Their Noble Mightinesses the Delegated Councilors understood that provided the burdened Mennonites made their marriage known to their Magistrates, confirmed it, and had it recorded, they would provisionally suffice until further order from Their Noble Great Mightinesses. Their Noble Mightinesses gave a similar *Appointment* <note>original: "Appoinctement," a legal decree or ruling</note> regarding the Request of two Mennonite couples at Abbekerk in 1613. 11. On the Practice of Church Discipline.

The Church Ban <term>Kerkelyke Ban: a form of excommunication where a member is excluded from the community for sinful behavior</term> is very unusual among these Congregations. When a case subject to it was known and proven, such a person would voluntarily refrain from the Lord's Supper <term>Nachtmael: the celebration of Holy Communion</term>, without waiting for any formal Ban; and in due time, he would conversely seek readmission. Consequently, people have not been able to tell me with what Customs and Circumstances the Ban would be handled in the Congregation; and for that same reason, Readmission <note>original: "Wederaenneming"</note> is also something rare among them (*).

(*) It is true, as we noted previously, that Church Discipline <note>original: "Kerkelyke Tugt"</note> has greatly slackened among the Mennonites <term>Doopsgezinden: literally "baptism-minded," the common Dutch term for Mennonites</term>. However, it does not seem so entirely out of use that one would not know how to say, as the Author remarks here, how the Practice of the Ban and Readmission is exercised among them. From what I have learned, there is no fixed rule for it; but the cases in which it has taken place in our time correspond closely with what occurs among other fellow believers. Someone who goes astray in a Public Sin of the Flesh <note>This is a reference to the "works of the flesh" listed in the Bible in Galatians 5:19, such as immorality or drunkenness</note>, and continues after the first, or also second and further admonition by the Teachers in private, is called before the Consistory <term>Kerkenraed: the governing council of the local church</term>; if he appears there, he is exhorted to repentance; if he refuses to come, they proceed to address him through the Church. If one or the other does not help, he is either suspended or cut off by the Consistory, with the approval of the Congregation, or the Brotherhood is requested to remain behind after the end of the Service. One of the Teachers first demonstrates from the Holy Scripture the necessity and goals of the Ban, namely the Reformation of the Sinner and the Fending off of Blame from the Congregation. Whereupon the Consistory, after the Invocation of God’s Name, with the Brotherhood, either suspends such a person from the use of the Lord's Supper, or even, depending on the case, cuts them off from the Congregation, until such time as he reforms; yet with this precaution, that one should not regard him as an Enemy but admonish him as a Brother. However, evidence of the latter has still been seen even if no actual Ban <term>Ban: a formal exclusion from the church community</term> had preceded it. For example, in the case of Members <term>Lidmaeten: individuals who have been baptized and admitted to full communion</term> who had defected to the Roman Catholic Church. Following this, they were brought by the Church Council before the Brotherhood <note>original: "Broederschap": the assembly of male members of the congregation who voted on church matters</note>; and they themselves publicly begged them to forgive the offense committed, while at the same time promising improvement for the future. The Presiding Minister of the Church Council then informed the Congregation that the Overseers <term>Opzienders: another term for the elders or leaders who watched over the spiritual well-being of the flock</term> were inclined to accept this Penitent back as a Member of the Congregation, provided the Brotherhood had nothing to bring against it. Since this latter did not happen and was not customary to happen, the silence of the Brothers was accepted as their consent. The Minister then called the Penitent (male or female) to come forward again and wel-

<meta>catchword: wel- (likely completing "welkom," meaning welcome)</meta>

---

<note>This section appears to be a clarifying footnote or an addition responding to the main text</note>

...[such as] Fornication or Adultery, etc. Regarding *Readmission* <note>original: "Wederaenneming"</note>, it proceeds roughly as the Author says, though with this distinction: that the Penitent also reports themselves beforehand to one of the Overseers, who then brings the request to the Church Council. Knowing no reason for refusal, the Penitent then appears in a subsequent session, expressing regret before the Church Council and requesting to be Readmitted. The Church Council presents that Request to the Brothers on the following Sunday; if they agree, then in a third session, in the name of the Church Council and by means of a heartfelt and compassionate Exhortation with a suitable Blessing, the Penitent is Readmitted by one of the Ministers. This Readmission is publicly announced from the Pulpit <note>original: "Predikstoel"</note> to the assembled multitude on the following Sunday.

<margin>
12. Concerning
House
Visits.
</margin>
Finally, regarding the church administration, I have this to note: the Members of each Church in large cities are divided into certain districts <note>original: "Wyken"</note> according to the number of Ministers, based on the specific parts or neighborhoods of the city. Each Teacher <term>Leeraer: a term used by Mennonites for their ministers or pastors</term> goes around his district once a year and conducts a *House Visit* (*) with all the members. However, the Ministers rotate these districts with one another every year and do not always keep the same ones. The Lutherans and Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Dutch Reformed Church, the public church of the Dutch Republic</note> also follow this custom. Through this rotation, the prejudices of certain people are often prevented. The Ministers also visit the sick, each within his own assigned district.

---

(*) This *House Visit* <note>original: "Huisbezoek"</note> does not occur everywhere among the Mennonites <term>Doopsgezinden: literally 'baptism-minded,' the standard Dutch term for Mennonites</term>; and its actual purpose is to invite the Members to participate in the Holy Supper <term>Avondmael: the celebration of communion</term>, and to exhort them to a thorough self-examination before that Holy Exercise. At the same time, it serves as an opportunity to settle any discord <note>original: "onmin"</note> that might have arisen between brother and brother, and to encourage young people, who are not yet part of the Congregation, to investigate the Truth, or even, where they feel the need, to request Holy Water Baptism.

The church buildings of these congregations do not have the appearance of churches from the outside; however, they are built with sufficient skill and appropriateness on the inside. The *Frisian-Teefsche* <note>The "Vries-Teefsche" were a specific, stricter subgroup of the Frisian Mennonites named after a prominent leader, Jan Teef.</note> congregation in Amsterdam has its church on the Princegragt [Prinsengracht] near the Princeftraet [Prinsenstraat]. Afterwards, this same building also served the *Collegiants* <term>Collegianten: a 17th-century Dutch religious group that allowed any member to speak and rejected formal clergy</term> for such a purpose (*); but it has since been sold and finally came into the possession of the *Frisian Mennonites*. I mention this here so that one might understand a certain passage relating to this in the excellent *Description of Amsterdam* by *Commelyn*, which consists of two folio volumes. This congregation currently (†) consists of no more than one hundred and fifty baptized members; yet, despite that small number, it possesses fine *ecclesiastical income*, and can therefore subsist very well and provide for the needs of its destitute members. It has no *orphanage*; and therefore places the children... <note>The sentence ends abruptly here as it continues on the next page.</note>

For this reason, the Secretary must always be from the Congregation where the Assembly is to be held.

<margin>3. Of the United Flemish and Waterlanders, and their Society meetings.</margin> The United Flemish and Waterlander Congregations—among which one must also include those consisting solely of Waterlanders or solely of Flemish <note>These were originally distinct sub-groups of Mennonites who later merged in many regions</note>—are too numerous throughout the United Netherlands to easily hold such a mutual Assembly every year. Thus, for example, in Leeuwarden in Friesland, a Society meeting is held annually on the first Friday after Pentecost—

[Gen]eral Deacons are asked whether they can manage with the amount previously raised, and whether they confirm this or indicate that more is needed; in both cases, each of the wealthy Congregations is asked what they would be pleased to contribute toward it. This is then reported by their Delegates, according to the instructions they have received for that purpose. All of this takes place in the *First Place*. The *Second* concerns the Travel Expenses of the Ministers. The *Third* is for other matters that have arisen and been recorded. The *Fourth* is for the Future Assembly.

The **Moravian Brethren** <note>original: "Hernnhuthers," a Pietist movement from Herrnhut</note> are infiltrating here and there among them. However tolerant these may be, they nevertheless want the Doctrine of the **Holy Trinity**, of **Grace**, of **Original Sin**, of **Justification**, and the like, to be understood in their own way, which is certainly not the way of the **Remonstrant-leaning** <note>Those favoring a more liberal, less dogmatic theology influenced by Arminianism</note> members. <margin>6. How these Parties behave toward one another.</margin>
The two types of **United Congregations**, as well as the **Frisians** <note>A more traditionalist and conservative subgroup of Mennonites</note>, are not well-disposed toward each other at heart, and here and there a fire seems to smolder under the ashes, which it is to be hoped can be extinguished through Prudence. # SECTION VI.

->*Of the Connection of all Mennonites with one another;*<-

<margin>VI. CONNECTION AND NUMBER OF ALL MENNONITE CONGREGATIONS.</margin>
The collective Mennonites <note>original: "Doopsgezinden," literally 'baptism-minded,' the name by which Mennonites are known in the Netherlands</note> of the two main branches, and the minor subdivisions among them described by me thus far—whether they belong to the so-called *Coarse* <note>original: "Groove," referring to the more liberal or world-facing branch</note> or the so-called *Fine* <note>original: "Fyne," referring to the more traditionalist or strict branch</note> Mennonites—have no fixed or definite assembly or formal connection. When necessity requires it, however, both the United Flemish and Waterlanders, together with the Frisian congregation, are entitled to write to the collective congregations of the United Netherlands and request that they appear in Amsterdam through delegates on a certain appointed day, in order to deal with the matters described in the summons. And according to that summons, they assemble from all over. The primary reason why such a meeting might be arranged nowadays is the distress of foreign coreligionists who require some assistance. For example, when they were driven out and persecuted in Switzerland, or from the Palatinate <note>original: "Paltz," a region in southwestern Germany</note>, or from Prussia, or elsewhere. For the management and oversight of the relief funds <note>original: "Onderstandgelden"</note> which are contributed by every congregation for the service of such needy and persecuted people, they have chosen two Teachers <note>original: "Leeraers," the traditional Mennonite term for ministers or pastors</note> and several Deacons from the Amsterdam congregations of both the United Waterlanders and Flemish, and one or two from the Church Council <note>original: "Kerkenraed"</note> of the Frisian congregation.

In short; they are a denomination which, regarding either its internal arrangement or its outward appearance, yields nothing to any other denomination in these lands, but rather claims all the privileges of the others for itself. The protection of the Government, along with the Mennonites' scholarship, wealth, and great numbers, maintains them in those advantages.

<margin>The attitude of the Mennonite and Reformed Ministers toward one another.</margin>
The Old Flemings, Frisians, and Mennonite Waterlanders and Flemings—or as they more often call themselves, the Orthodox <note>original: "Regtzinnige," meaning "straight-thinking" or doctrinally sound</note> Mennonites—stand in good friendship with the Ministers and Advocates of the Reformed Church, at least outwardly. In their writings, their Ministers speak of the Reformed Pastors and Professors with much respect, and these, in turn, mention those Mennonite Ministers with much courtesy. However, regarding the other United Waterlander and Flemish Congregations, which I have called the Remonstrant-minded <note>These were Mennonites who sympathized with the Remonstrants (Arminians), who disagreed with the strict Calvinist views on predestination</note>, one must think a little differently. # Introduction of the MENNONITES.

...the Gospel is suited to set itself against Errors.
<margin>STATE OF AFFAIRS UNTO THE DISPUTES.</margin>
One will judge this with Love all the more readily when one considers that truth-loving men give place to their zeal against Errors in all kinds of ways (*); while they nevertheless believe they are pursuing a laudable cause out of a desire for the Salvation of Mankind and the Glory of GOD. But, be that as it may, I shall not occupy myself now with any further citation of the Sources from which such Actions flow, nor with mentioning many pieces that might serve as some proof, but I turn much rather to my Purpose: namely, the Account of the Course of the Newest Conflict which, in a Matter of a similar nature as I have cited until now, has arisen in the United Netherlands, and is not yet entirely at an end.

<margin>Arrival of the Socinians in the Netherlands.</margin>
Now, so that the matter may be understood all the more clearly, I must first report that the Socinian Sect <note>The Socinians were a rationalist Christian group that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ; they were often persecuted by both Catholics and traditional Protestants.</note>, from the time of its origin until today, has always attempted to gain a firm footing in these Lands; yet it has never yet been able to achieve its objective. Already at the end of the Sixteenth Century, General Regulations were made against them. Of their Doctrine, it was publicly asserted that it agreed most of all with the Position of the Muha- <note>The catchword "me-" indicates the word continues as "Muhammedanen" (Mohammedans). In this period, critics of Socinianism often compared it to Islam because both faiths emphasized the absolute oneness of God.</note>

THE STATE OF AFFAIRS UNTIL THE DISPUTES.
Dismay among them regarding this.

One can easily understand that this Decree caused great dismay and commotion among the <term>Mennonites</term> <note>original: "Doopsgezinden"; a Protestant group practicing adult baptism, often known for their pacifism and refusal to swear oaths</note> in general. It grieved them deeply that the High Authority—acting on the proposal of church governors from outside the Mennonite community—exercised this power over their internal and ecclesiastical affairs. This effectively allowed for a kind of <term>Investigation of Faith</term> <note>original: "Onderzoek des Geloofs"; a formal inquiry into a person's religious beliefs, similar to an inquisition</note>, even if that was not the original intent. Documents were presented to the Mennonite Teachers to sign which no Mennonite, regardless of their faction, could sign with such directness and without reservation, unless they were willing to abandon the <term>Confessions</term> <note>Traditional statements of faith or creeds handed down through generations</note> of their ancestors. As I have mentioned before, all Mennonites have always refrained from using the word *Person* when discussing the Mystery of the Holy Trinity.

Furthermore, it was believed that someone could hold views contrary to the specific points presented in these Articles without necessarily being a *Socinian* <note>A follower of a doctrine that rejected the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ; at the time, being labeled a Socinian could lead to legal trouble or banishment</note>. One might judge these matters in the manner of the *Remonstrants* <note>Dutch Protestants who disagreed with the strict Calvinist views on predestination</note> or in the tradition of various Great Teachers of the *English Church* <note>The Anglican Church</note>. Surely, according to the founding principles of the Dutch State, this could not be forbidden to anyone? By pushing for this, the <term>Reformed Clergy</term> <note>The ministers of the official state-sanctioned church in the Netherlands</note> ran the risk of being suspected of wanting to use the <term>Edicts</term> <note>original: "Plakaeten"; formal laws or decrees issued by the government</note> created against the *Socinians* as a way to define and restrict any other denominations that happened to displease them. However, it would be wrong to attribute such specific motives to any individual; I declare once more that I am merely recording as a <term>Historian</term> what was thought at the time.

After some disputes of small importance, there finally arose the public and great dispute, of which I shall now relate the most necessary and essential parts.

### Part I. OF THE MENNONITES.

<margin>
THE CASE OF THE TEACHERS OF HEERENVEEN.
</margin>

...to submit regarding their inner convictions. Namely, they believe that thoughts and inner feelings do not fall under the reach of the Secular Power, as the latter only concerns itself with the outward condition of men; and they appeal in this regard to several Great Jurists (*). They believe that as Christians they can suffice with a General Confession and acknowledgment of the truth and divinity of the Holy Scripture, and of all that is taught therein as necessary for Salvation. They hold the wording of the Holy Scripture to be the most fitting to express the Divine Doctrine; and they consider all other interpretations and wordings proposed by men to be only of a human authority, and not binding to the conscience. And therefore they believe that one cannot reasonably require someone to submit themselves entirely to such human concepts; especially not if he has not yet made himself guilty of <term>Socinian<gloss>A rationalist Christian movement that rejected the doctrine of the Trinity; in this period, it was a common accusation used to label someone a heretic.</gloss></term> propositions <margin>* Has not yet made himself suspect.</margin> *. It seems to them that such an inquiry tastes of the hateful word *Inquisition* <note>original: "Inquisitie"; a reference to the Catholic ecclesiastical courts used to suppress heresy, a highly charged term in the Protestant Netherlands</note>; they believe that this manner exposes them to the constant attacks of power-hungry and envious people, and that all this runs counter to the Freedom for which their ancestors suffered and fought so much. For the rest, they testify to being ready to give an account of everything they have taught, whether publicly or in private; they trust that they will easily show the vanity <note>meaning the lack of legal merit or substance</note> of the accusations brought against them; and they offer themselves, in case they can be convicted <meta>wor-</meta> <note>the Dutch word "worden" (to be/become) is split across the page break</note>

### CURRENT STATE III. Chapter III.

<margin>THE CASE OF THE TEACHERS OF HEERENVEEN.</margin>
...[to be found guilty] of having spread <term>Socinian<gloss>Followers of a rationalist theology that denied the Trinity; in the 18th century, this was a serious charge of heresy.</gloss></term> teachings, and to willingly undergo the penalties and fines established for that purpose by the Edicts of the Land.

<margin>Verdict of the Honorable and Mighty States-Deputies.</margin>
The two Honorable Commissioners took great offense at this document. In their Report or Account to the Honorable and Mighty States-Deputies (*), they declared it to be a **calumnious libel**, filled with all kinds of hateful words and lies, in which they were falsely portrayed as having conducted an inquiry of faith regarding these men that was entirely unrelated to the actual accusations—an inquiry which they utterly detest. They took great issue with the word ***Inquisition*** <note>original: "Inquisitie"; a highly provocative term in the Protestant Dutch Republic, as it likened the local authorities to the feared Catholic religious courts</note> and demanded a *suitable satisfaction* <note>original: "convenable Satisfactie"</note>, or proper restitution. The verdict of the Honorable and Mighty Lords States-Deputies, which followed this (†), consisted mainly of the approval of everything the aforementioned Honorable Commissioners had done. Wybe Pieters, because he had declared himself orthodox, was readmitted to his preaching service. But regarding the two other Mennonite teachers, it was ruled that, as they were suspected of being guilty of the "horrible and blasphemous sentiments of <term>Socinus<gloss>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), whose teachings questioned the divinity of Christ and were officially banned.</gloss></term>," they were forbidden from the office of teacher and would not be readmitted until they showed themselves willing and prepared to answer the accusations against them clearly and in person.

The aforementioned Verdict brought the Mennonite congregations [of Friesland] into great unrest, and caused them much concern for the future (*). Besides this, it had come to their attention that at the last meeting of the aforementioned Classis, a proposal had been made to initiate such an investigation against Mennonite teachers in *general* (§). # II. Section. OF THE MENNONITES.

<margin>
THE DEDUCTION, etc. Their Petition and Deduction submitted to the Assembly of the States.
</margin>

But when, in the first month of the following year, 1740, the Noble and Mighty Lords, the States of Friesland, were assembled in Leeuwarden for the annual <term>Landdag<gloss>An assembly of the estates of a province, similar to a regional parliament or diet.</gloss></term>, the delegates of these <term>Congregations<gloss>Refers to the Mennonite or 'Doopsgezinde' communities.</gloss></term> submitted a *Petition* or Supplication (*) according to the resolution of a Church Assembly (though a few congregations did not involve themselves with it).

In this document, they recounted the recent events in their own manner and, in the name of their collective congregations, requested that their **Noble Mightinesses**, the Lords of the States of Friesland, would be pleased to exempt them and their Teachers in the future from all examination, <term>Confession of Faith<gloss>Here meaning a compulsory, standardized statement of doctrine that one must sign to be considered 'orthodox.'</gloss></term>, and the signing of Human Articles, whether before secular or ecclesiastical courts. They sought this so that they would not be forced to do anything that conflicted with their consciences, and so they would not be constantly troubled and condemned based on frivolous accusations and empty suspicions. 

To make this request of theirs all the more acceptable, they saw fit to attach to this *Petition* a reasonably extensive document called a *Deduction* <note>original: "Deductie"—a formal legal statement of facts and arguments submitted to a court or government body.</note> or *More Detailed Argument*. Through this, they endeavored to prove that their aforementioned request was in accordance with: 1. The Original Rights of Nature; 2. Divine Revelation; and 3. The Foundations of the Dutch State. They further asserted that it is the duty of all true Christians in general, and of Protestants in particular, to hold the Holy Scriptures as the only rule of faith and doctrine, and not to bind oneself to any prescriptions or opinions of fallible men. They maintained,

<margin>III. Concerning the OPINIONS of the THEOLOGICAL FACULTIES and Church CLASSES, especially that of Professor VENEMA. Unrest in Friesland regarding Pastor Stinstra's Sermons.</margin>
All the writings mentioned thus far were essays by private and individual persons. I must therefore go back a little and relate what was submitted and said following the directive of the High Authorities regarding the sermons of *Stinstra*. Because those sermons had been published, the ministers of the Reformed Church <note>The "Gereformeerde Kerk" was the public, state-supported church in the Dutch Republic, which held significant influence over religious and social life.</note> could by no means remain silent; for the events of the previous year were therein rebuked too severely, although not in explicit words. Pressure was therefore applied, not only at the Meetings of the Classis <term>Classis: a regional governing body in the Reformed Church composed of ministers and elders from a specific district</term> but also at the Synod <term>Synod: a larger ecclesiastical assembly; in this case, the provincial gathering in the city of Bolsward</term> of Bolsward, to ensure this matter was addressed. And the delegates from Groningen, who had been sent to the Synod according to custom, supported this plan to the best of their ability. Now, there were some who claimed that this case properly belonged to the Magistrate of the city of Harlingen—where those sermons had been delivered and printed and where the author lived—rather than to the Honorable and Mighty Lords of the Delegated States <term>Delegated States: the executive committee of the provincial government (Provincial States) that handled administrative and legal matters between full legislative sessions</term>. However, the other party rejected this; it was unknown how the city Magistrate would view this matter, and whether the Reformed clergy would be sufficiently heard there, since Mr. *Stinstra* had made many friends for himself in that place. [States therefore] deemed it good to bring the Sermons of *Stinstra* under investigation; and to that end, on June 17, 1741, they issued a summons to the five Theological Faculties of the Netherlands—namely at *Leiden*, *Utrecht*, *Harderwijk*, *Franeker*, and *Groningen*—to obtain their thoughts and opinions regarding *Stinstra’s* book. The six Classes <term>Classes: The regional governing bodies of the Dutch Reformed Church, composed of ministers and elders from a specific district</term> of the Reformed Ministers in Friesland—namely the Classes of *Leeuwarden*, *Dokkum*, *Franeker*, *Sneek*, *Bolsward*, and *Zevenwouden*—were also ordered to likewise provide their opinions. The objections arrived from all sides, concluding (*) that the Sermons of Mr. *Stinstra* could not be entirely cleared of Socinian <term>Socinian: A theological movement that emphasized reason and rejected the traditional doctrine of the Trinity; in the 18th century, it was a serious charge of heresy used against those seen as too rationalist</term> propositions, and were therefore to be regarded as a harmful book. For these reasons, I have decided—so that the honored reader may have a closer understanding of these Sermons—to <insert>include</insert> the essence of the objections of the famous Professor here...

### THE CURRENT STATE [OF THE UNITED NETHERLANDS] SECTION III. CHAPTER III.

<margin>ADVICE OF VENEMA.</margin>
> GOD, as a righteous judge and avenger of sin, has been satisfied <note>This refers to the doctrine of "Satisfaction," where Christ's death pays the debt of human sin to God's justice.</note>, yet has only assured humans both of the truth of His Doctrine and of the grace of the Forgiveness of Sins along with Eternal Life, for all those who acknowledge Him and, with repentance for their sins, sincerely observe His Teachings and Commands.

— He [Venema] stipulates that if these Propositions are to be contained in any Book, they must either be found there in plain words, or be derived from it through such consequences that are so direct, clear, and certain that they can be denied by no one, or cannot be twisted by the Author except through violence; these consequences being: 1. That all that is said regarding Christ's Person and Glory refers *only* to His human nature; and 2. That Justification <note>The theological process by which a sinner is declared righteous before God.</note> is granted *only* out of grace, on account of faith and good works.

<margin>What is insufficient to judge a text as Socinian.</margin>
Upon this, the Professor proceeds and shows how this implies; *Firstly*, that one does not have sufficient reason to declare a Book to be Socinian <term>Socinian: A follower of Socinus; a 17th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, emphasizing His role as a moral teacher.</term> when it passes over in silence the Truths which oppose the main Socinian errors, even if it appeared to us that they ought to have been discussed, and we ourselves certainly would not have omitted those Doctrines in such a case. For to prove a *factum* <note>original: "Factum" — a Latin legal term meaning a "fact" or an "act" that has been committed.</note>, or something that has been done, positive proof is required: it is not the concealment of the opposite, but the explicit mention of a Proposition that makes someone guilty. The concealment of a proposition can arise from causes other than the denial of the matter. It can, namely, spring from the thought that such a point does not belong to the subject being treated,

### III. Part. OF THE MENNONITES.

<margin>ADVICE OF VENEMA.</margin>
*...to be intended to save the World or the Souls of Men, and to make Sinners blessed, and to reconcile them with GOD, etc.* <note>This continues the analysis of Stinstra's descriptions of Christ's purpose on earth.</note> The Lord Professor <note>Hermanus Venema (1697–1787), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note> admits that the Author <note>Johannes Stinstra</note> should have expressed himself more clearly if he had wished to prevent the suspicion of Socinianism <term>Socinianism: A rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity and the substitutionary atonement of Christ.</term>. However, it is to his advantage that elsewhere he distinguishes other objectives of Christ’s Incarnation, namely the Reconciliation with GOD, from his Teaching and Kingly Office; and that in this place he speaks *only* of the Walk of Christ among Men, and not of his Death. Now, this [his death] belongs chiefly to his Priestly Office; but his Walk among Men belongs to his Prophetic and Kingly Ministry. Therefore, seeing that the Writer has spoken only of the Objectives of Christ’s Walk on earth, he merely intended to bring forward its principal end and objective, and to show how it is said of Christ also as Prophet and King that He saves the Souls of Men, reconciles Sinners with GOD, etc.—namely, through his Doctrine. ### 236 PRESENT STATE III. Chapter.

<margin>ADVICE OF VENEMA.</margin>
...by no means; for the Doctrine of Christ is not excluded, but set as a guideline. Therefore, it is only asserted thereby that everyone must judge the Doctrine for themselves, and believe for their own salvation that which they find therein. And for this reason, Mr. *Stinstra* does not want the Socinians <note>A sect that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ; they were widely considered heretical at the time.</note> to be excluded from Christian Fellowship; just as *Locke* <note>John Locke (1632–1704), the English philosopher whose "Letter Concerning Toleration" was foundational to these debates.</note> desired, whom *Clericus* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Swiss theologian and prominent scholar in the Republic of Letters.</note> defended for that reason.

<margin>
4. Main Proposition.
</margin>
4. *Fourthly*, Lord *Venema* says, the Author intends to assert that every Christian has the Right, and is obligated, to investigate the points of Christian Doctrine themselves, and to submit blindly to no Human Prescriptions <note>Meaning man-made rules or creeds that have not been personally verified through Scripture.</note> in this regard: and this is a fundamental principle of the Protestants. *Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his moderate and irenic views.</note> is cited here.

<margin>
5. Main Proposition.
</margin>
5. *Fifthly*, the Author of the Sermons intends to assert, says the Lord Professor, that everyone has the Right to share their private thoughts on Divine Truths as well as other sciences with the world; provided that such does not result in the harm of good morals. Here a passage from *Thomas Burnet* <note>An English theologian (c. 1635–1715) who often clashed with orthodox authorities over his interpretations of sacred history.</note> is added. And the Lord Professor *Venema* concludes with the words that the Famous *Hermannus Witsius* <note>A highly respected Dutch Reformed theologian (1636–1708).</note> was accustomed to use:
> *Unity in essentials, liberty in non-essentials, in all things prudence and charity* <note>original: "In necessariis unitas, in non necessariis libertas, in omnibus prudentia & charitas"</note>; that is: "In the necessary things let one be in agreement, in the non-necessary things let one have freedom, in both let one use caution and love."

# VI. Part. OF THE MENNONITES.

<margin>REMARKS ON THE DISPUTES.</margin>
Likewise, the position of the <term>Reformed</term> <note>The state-supported Calvinist Church in the Dutch Republic.</note> Teachers displeases many: namely, that the Authorities perform a necessary duty when they entirely forbid the exercise of the <term>Socinian</term> <note>A non-trinitarian Christian movement that denied the divinity of Jesus; they were often viewed as radical heretics by both the Reformed and the Mennonites.</note> religion in their lands and never allow such a church gathering. It is well-conceded that there may be laws against foreign Socinians or those coming from abroad; however, it is believed that there is a third or middle way between the two diverging positions of the Reformed and the <term>Mennonites</term>. Namely, that the Authorities should not refuse their subjects a mutual exercise of their intended religion if some of them fall into Socinian errors by their own choice; yet, in the meantime, the rest of the Christians should not suffer or admit the Socinians into their own Church Communion and inner brotherhood. One cannot agree to two things: 1. That one must bear the Socinians in other congregations as spiritual brothers, or even as teachers. And 2. Not to grant them, in one way or another, their own and separate exercise of religion when they are subjects of the Land. It is asserted that the Mennonites, in their writings, have maintained the impropriety of the latter not without some appearance of reason, and that the Reformed, on the contrary, have excellently proven the absurdity of the former: but that the Mennonites applied the grounds against the second position to maintain the first, and the Reformed applied the grounds against the first position to assert the second, and thus both sides have deviated from the target. Indeed, the Mennonite writers have a doubly-absurd

# APPENDIX.

<margin>
HIGH GOVERNMENT OF FRIESLAND.
I. Of the Noble and Mighty Lords States, and the Provincial Diet.
</margin>

I shall say nothing here of the Noble and Mighty Lords States of the other provinces, though I could easily do so; instead, I shall only mention the High Government of the Province of Friesland. The Estates or Members of the High Government of Friesland comprise four Colleges. One of these consists of the *Eleven Cities* of this land. The three others are the three Quarters into which the countryside is divided. They are called: *Oostergo*, *Westergo*, and *Zevenwolden*. These regions are divided into <term>Grietenijen</term> <note>A 'grietenij' was a specifically Frisian administrative and judicial district, roughly equivalent to a bailiwick or rural municipality.</note>, that is, into bailiwicks or offices, which together number thirty. When the Estates of Friesland assemble—which happens every year—each Grietenij sends two persons, one from the Nobility and one from the rank of the rural commons, to Leeuwarden; each city likewise sends two delegates. All these deputies together make a total of eighty-two. However, they never meet in that full number in the same chamber; instead, they form four separate chambers, each of which confers on the matters at hand to determine a collective vote. To form a common Resolution of the entire body of the High Government, two persons are deputed from each chamber—and thus eight in total—to the Fifth Chamber, who deliberate and consider together until a Resolution is reached, either unanimously or by a majority of votes. For each chamber must be regarded as a unified body which carries no more than one vote, which may be called a College-vote, formed from many <term>collective votes</term> <margin>* From many <note>original: "Votis curiatis"</note> collective votes.</margin>. If the votes remain tied against one another, then no decision can be made. These assembled States represent the Majesty of Friesland, and depend

# APPENDIX.

<margin>HIGH GOVERNMENT OF FRIESLAND.</margin>
[This government] depends on no higher human authority. <note>Continuing the thought from the previous page, this emphasizes that the Frisian Estates held sovereign power, independent of any outside human ruler.</note> His Highness the Lord Hereditary <term>Stadhouder</term> <note>The chief executive and military commander of the province. In Friesland, this office was held by the branch of the House of Nassau-Diez.</note> of Friesland has the right to be present in the Fifth Chamber during the deliberations of the Eight Delegates; however, he does not have the power to decide the proceedings, but only to hear them.

<margin>2. Of the Noble and Mighty Delegated States, and the Hereditary Stadhouder.</margin>
When this <term>Landdag</term> <note>The Provincial Diet or annual assembly of the representatives of the cities and rural districts.</note> is about to conclude, each of the Chambers elects two Deputies; only the Chamber of the Cities elects three. These are called the Noble and Mighty Lords Delegated States, and they conduct the High Government of the land in the name of the entire Diet until the Noble and Mighty Lords States assemble again for the Diet in the following year: and His Highness the Lord Hereditary Stadhouder is the Supreme President of this High College. All the cities, with the exception of Franeker alone, have granted the Lord Hereditary Stadhouder the right to appoint their municipal officers. From this, it is easy to conclude that the three Lords Delegated States who are nominated by the cities are particularly well-disposed toward His Highness. That Prince holds the dignity of Governor or Stadhouder hereditarily, and receives 4,000 Dutch <term>Guilders</term> <note>The "Gulden" was the primary currency of the Dutch Republic.</note> annually from it. In addition, His Highness is Captain-General over the military forces and receives 5,000 Guilders from that office. For his household, he receives an additional 40,000 Guilders, and enjoys the income as Colonel of a regiment, etc.

## SECTION II.

### On the Government of the Dutch Reformed Church.

The government of the Reformed congregations in the United Netherlands is clearly <term>Presbyterian</term> <note>A system of church government by representative assemblies of elders, rather than by bishops.</note>. Each congregation has a <term>Consistory</term> <note>Dutch: *Kerkenraed*; the local governing council of a church.</note>. This consists of the <term>Ministers</term> <note>Dutch: *Predikanten*.</note>, as permanent members <gloss>assessing members</gloss>, chairs <gloss>presidents</gloss>, and writers <gloss>scribes</gloss> of the Consistory. They rotate the presidency and the office of scribe every month, or sometimes in an even shorter period. The other leaders are the <term>Elders</term> <note>Dutch: *Ouderlingen*.</note>; and in many congregations, also the <term>Deacons</term> <note>Dutch: *Diakonen*; officials responsible for the care of the poor.</note>. The Elders and Deacons are chosen by the Consistory; they remain in their service for two years and then make way for others. One can easily understand that this constant rotation increases the prestige of the Ministers, as they are the only permanent members.

In prominent cities, besides this Consistory, there are also <term>Churchwardens</term> <note>Dutch: *Kerk-Meesters*.</note> who have oversight of the church building and the burial sites within it. In the Consistory, ecclesiastical matters are handled: for example, proselytes <note>Those converting to the faith from another belief system.</note> who convert from unbelief to the Christian religion among the Reformed are examined there; ecclesiastical <term>attestations</term> <note>Dutch: *Attestatiën*; formal certificates of membership used when moving between congregations.</note> are drawn up there; sinners are also rebuked there or cut off from the congregation; the latter, however, cannot occur without the approval of the <term>Classis</term> <note>A regional governing body composed of ministers and elders from several neighboring churches.</note>. There, Ministers who have fallen into a grave sin can be suspended from their service, though not without the knowledge...

<margin>2. Regarding the Classical Assemblies.</margin>
One can appeal the judgment of the Consistory to the Classis. A Classis is essentially an <term>Ecclesiastical Sub-district</term> <note>Dutch: *Kerkelyk Smaldeel*.</note>, consisting of a certain number of churches situated in proximity to one another. Each Province is divided into several such Classes. The Classical Assemblies consist of two delegates from each of the churches belonging to the Classis. These delegates are a <term>Minister</term> <note>Dutch: *Predikant*.</note> and an Elder. They bring from their Consistory a <term>Credential</term> <note>original Latin/Dutch: *Credentiael*.</note> and <term>Instruction</term> <note>original: *Instructie*.</note>, or as I would call it in German, a <term>Power of Attorney</term> <note>original: *Volmagt*.</note>. Three to seven such Classical Assemblies are held annually. The location of the meeting rotates in turns; the same applies to the offices of <term>President</term> <note>original: *President*; Chairperson.</note> and <term>Scribe</term> <note>original: *Scriba*; Secretary or Clerk.</note>. At these meetings, arrangements are made for <term>Ecclesiastical Discipline</term> <note>Dutch: *Kerkelyken Tugt*; the system of maintaining moral and doctrinal standards among members.</note>; care is provided for the poor, for schools, etc.; the complaints of those who believe themselves aggrieved by the judgment of the Consistory here or there are heard. One *examines* or investigates those who wish to become <term>Candidates</term> <note>original: *Proponenten*; those who have finished their studies and are permitted to preach but not yet ordained to a specific church.</note>, that is, those admitted to preach and offer themselves for the ministry; one elects those who will attend the Provincial <term>Synod</term> <note>original: *Synodus*.</note>, or the church assembly of the province, on behalf of each Classis. At these Classical Assemblies, the election of the <term>Visitors</term> <note>original: *Visitatoren*.</note> also takes place—that is, those who annually inspect the condition of the churches and schools. <margin>3. Regarding the Provincial Synods.</margin>
The Provincial Church Assemblies or *Synods* consist of delegated leaders from the churches of an entire province, and they meet only once a year. In Zeeland alone, this *Synod*, or—as that assembly is called there—the <term>Coetus</term> <note>original: *Cœtus*; a Latin term for a gathering or meeting.</note> is not held at set times, but only upon important occurrences by the order of the <term>States of Zeeland</term> <note>The sovereign provincial government of the region.</note>. To the Provincial Church Assemblies, not every congregation, but only each <term>Classis</term> <note>A regional administrative body of the church.</note> sends delegates: namely, two or three <term>Ministers</term> <note>Dutch: *Predikanten*.</note> and one or two <term>Elders</term> <note>Dutch: *Ouderlingen*.</note>; although no elders attend the *Synod* of the region of Drenthe. These delegates must have attended the most recent Classical meeting, and therefore be best informed regarding the affairs of the Classis.

The *President* or Chairman of the church assembly of the previous year, or perhaps a <term>Deputy</term> <note>original: *Deputatus*; a representative appointed to act on behalf of the Synod between sessions.</note> of the Synod (of whom more shortly), opens the meeting with a prayer, receives the *Credentials* or powers of attorney, and holds the office of Chairman until a new one is chosen; which occurs immediately after these first formalities. Alongside the *President*, an *Assessor*—that is an assistant or Vice-President—as well as a <term>Scribe</term> <note>original: *Scriba*; the secretary or clerk responsible for the minutes.</note> is elected. Once this is done, they can proceed to the Synodal Transactions. At each Synod, two delegates of the clergy appear from each of the other provinces of the <term>United State</term> <note>Referring to the United Provinces of the Netherlands.</note>. They are always appointed at the Synod of the province from which they will go to the Synods of the others. They bear the name of *Correspondents*: and are present there to [maintain] the unity of the...

4. Concerning the Number of these Synods, and the Walloon Synod.

In the United Netherlands, nine such Synods or church assemblies are held; for the entire Republic actually consists of nine states (†), of which the second and third are forever united with one another in worldly matters <note>This refers to South Holland and North Holland, which functioned as a single political province (Holland) but maintained two separate ecclesiastical synods.</note>. The region of Drenthe is a distinct state, which has no seat or vote in the assembly of the <term>States-General</term> <note>original: *Algemeene Staeten*; the federal government of the Dutch Republic.</note>. Besides these, the French—or rather the <term>Walloon</term> <note>Protestant refugees from the Spanish Netherlands.</note> and <term>Huguenot</term> <note>French Protestant refugees.</note>—congregations of the United Netherlands hold a General Church Assembly twice every year, which maintains brotherhood with the <term>Dutch</term> <note>original: *Nederduitsche*; literally 'Low German,' the historical term for the Dutch language and the main Reformed Church.</note> Synods, yet is separate on account of language and is in no way subject to them.

A National Church Assembly <note>Also known as a National Synod.</note> was to be proposed by the clergy of the Reformed Church in the collective Netherlands, and was to be held every three years; though not without the consent of the High Authorities <note>The civil government, specifically the States-General.</note>. NUMBER OF THE CONGREGATIONS etc.
3. Of the [Religious] Denominations.
</margin>
In the United Netherlands, one finds Two hundred seventy-five Roman Catholic Congregations, which are served by approximately Four hundred Priests. But besides these, there is a large number of Roman congregations in the <term>Lands of the Generality</term> <note>The *Generaliteitslanden* were territories conquered by the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years' War, governed directly by the States-General rather than having their own provincial government; these areas remained predominantly Catholic.</note>, which is that part of Flanders and Brabant that is subject to the Republic. Thirty-three Congregations and Seventy-four Priests are always *Jansenist* <note>Followers of a theological movement initiated by Cornelius Jansen, which emphasized original sin and divine grace; in the Netherlands, this led to the formation of the Old Catholic Church after a break with Rome.</note>. They have a Jansenist Archbishop and Chapter in Utrecht, and additionally Two Archpriests and Two Archdeacons. All the remaining Roman Congregations and Priests are *Constitutionists* <note>Those who accepted the papal bull *Unigenitus* (the "Constitution") issued by Pope Clement XI in 1713, which condemned Jansenism.</note>, that is, those who have accepted the Constitution of Pope Clement XI. Among them are Fifteen Archpriests. Many of the Priests are members of Orders, whether they be Friars Minor <note>Also known as Franciscans.</note>, Dominicans, Jesuits, Augustinians, and so forth. However, they do not wear the Habit of their Order when they appear on the street.

<margin>
4. Of the Remonstrants.
</margin>
The <term>Remonstrants</term> <note>A liberal Protestant group that separated from the Dutch Reformed Church in the early 17th century, following the views of Jacobus Arminius on predestination.</note> have Thirty-four Congregations in the Netherlands, and one in Fredrikstad <note>Located in modern-day Norway; it was a site of refuge for Remonstrants during their persecution.</note>, which is provided for by the Society of this Country with a Minister, and also with support and money. These Congregations have Forty-four Ministers. Besides this, they have a <term>Seminary</term> <note>original: *Queekſchool*. Literally a "nursery school," used here in the sense of a training college for clergy.</note> in Amsterdam, in which there are two Professors. One has Sixteen hundred, the other Thirteen hundred Guilders as an annual Salary. The Remonstrant Ministers in the primary Congregations receive as much as the first-mentioned Professor: but in the others, it is in proportion; much like the Reformed, and sometimes even a bit less.

## ACCOUNT.

### I.

->*Regarding their Meetings at Rijnsburg.*<-

The Society of the **COLLEGIANTS** or **RIJNSBURGERS** <note>Also known as "Rijnsburgers" because their most important gatherings, particularly for baptism by immersion, took place in the village of Rijnsburg near Leiden.</note> meets twice a year in Rijnsburg, a village outside Leiden. The first time is at Pentecost; the second meeting [which is on the last Sunday of August] coincides with the Rotterdam Fair or Annual Market <note>A "Kermis" was both a church festival and a secular fair; the Rotterdam market was one of the largest in the region.</note>: it is likely scheduled at that time, partly because many from Rotterdam gladly go out to the countryside during such a period to escape the noise and bustle; partly because it is then the most pleasant time for travel; and partly because many strangers <note>Visitors or foreigners from outside the immediate community.</note> come to the vicinity of Rijnsburg on the mentioned occasion.

## II.

### *Regarding their Name.*

[They are named *Rijnsburgers* after this place of their General Assembly; and *Collegiants* after their mutual meetings <note>The name "Collegiants" comes from the Latin "collegia," referring to the private, informal gatherings or "colleges" where they met to study Scripture without a presiding minister.</note>.] They were formerly called by their opponents the *New Sect of Prophets*, with reference to 1 Corinthians 14 <note>This chapter of the Bible discusses "prophesying," which the Collegiants interpreted as the right of any member of the congregation to speak or preach, rather than just an ordained minister.</note>. But they absolutely reject that name; nor is it any longer in use. The ignorant multitude in Rijnsburg gives them the name of *Quakers*; [yet entirely without reason <note>During this period, "Quaker" was often used as a catch-all slur for any religious group that rejected formal church hierarchy, despite the Collegiants having distinct beliefs from the Society of Friends.</note>.]

## III.

### *Regarding their Origin.*

[Concerning the beginning of the Collegiants, which is set at the year 1619, the following should be noted.] The Remonstrants <note>A liberal group of Dutch Protestants who were expelled from the state church following the Synod of Dordrecht; they disagreed with the strict doctrine of predestination.</note>, in later times when they themselves had gained a firm footing in Holland, viewed the Collegiants as a party that had separated from them, and therefore thought it their duty above all others to bring these stray sheep back to the right path. For this reason, they also published various writings against that society. However, the Collegiants will not admit this. They say that, before the holding and ending of the Synod of Dordrecht <note>The 1618–1619 national council of the Dutch Reformed Church which condemned the Remonstrant views and led to the exile or removal of many liberal ministers.</note>, there was no distinct denomination or church of Remonstrants, but that the believers in Universal Grace <note>The theological position that God's grace and salvation are available to all people, not just a chosen few.</note> as teachers and listeners [were found] here and there among the Reformed...

->PRESENT STATE<-

[...remained in the majority], and have always maintained church fellowship with them. It was indeed true that these confessors of Universal Grace <note>Original: "Algemeene Genade." This is the theological belief that God's grace is offered to all humanity, contrasting with the "limited atonement" or strict predestination of the Reformed state church.</note> had already received the name of Remonstrants previously, yet they did not for that reason constitute a separate Church: to such an extent, even, that Remonstrant teachers were found among Counter-Remonstrant audiences, and Counter-Remonstrant teachers among Remonstrant audiences. 

But after the Synod <note>The Synod of Dordrecht (1618–1619), a national assembly of the Dutch Reformed Church held to settle the controversy over Arminianism/Remonstrantism.</note> had cut off the Remonstrant teachers and members from the Reformed Church, and the High Authority <note>The "Hooge Overigheid," referring to the States-General or the regional governing bodies of the Netherlands.</note> had given legal authority to the decisions of this church assembly, those who cherished Universal Grace were forced to come to a separate ecclesiastical arrangement. The brothers *van der Kodde*, along with their good friends, consequently immediately established a religious society, which was called the Collegiant society, and in which all spiritual exercises, including Baptism and the Lord’s Supper, flourished before the present-day Remonstrants had grown into a separate Church. 

For the rest of those who were cut off spent some time in exile and dispersion; but finally, when they obtained a little more freedom, they created an ecclesiastical arrangement of an entirely different form; and this is what is now called the Remonstrant Church. Furthermore, it would appear from the time at which the Collegiant society arose that they cannot be presented as a splinter party of the Remonstrants that sprouted and went out from their Church. The same is also evident when one considers the views and opinions [of both] in religious matters. The brothers *van der Kodde* agreed with the Remonstrants in...

## IV.

### *About the Brothers van der Kodde.*

[These Brothers *van der Kodde*, named *Jan*, *Adriaen*,
and *Gysbregt*, lived in *Oegstgeest*, *Rijnsburg*, and *Warmond*,] all [three]

that is, Willem’s son. He left eight Children 
behind. Before the light of the Gospel fully

Added to this was the fact that the Collegiants found a great deal to criticize in many of the Remonstrant Preachers. For the lifestyle of these Teachers, which was not always precisely the best, could not remain unknown to the people during the time of Persecution, seeing as the people often had to harbor them in secret. In particular, the Collegiants could not approve of the conduct of the Remonstrants where they thought to establish themselves here and there with Force and Weapons (*); while some advocated for absolute Non-resistance <term>Lydzaemheit: A Dutch term used by groups like the Mennonites to describe "patient endurance" or "long-suffering," specifically referring to a commitment to pacifism and refusing to use force even when persecuted.</term> along with the Mennonites. These and other similar circumstances rendered all proposals for Union fruitless.

<margin>A. From the distinction between the unity of the Invisible Church and that of the Visible Church.</margin>
The **Unity of the Invisible Church** <note>In Protestant theology, the "Invisible Church" refers to the spiritual body of all true believers known only to God, while the "Visible Church" refers to the earthly organizations of believers.</note> does not take away the diversity of the **Visible Churches**. According to the degree that one agrees much or little with one another, one also has more or less in common; and thus the bonds of that society are broader or narrower. If two persons both fear **GOD**, each in his own way, but otherwise share only the **Holy Scripture** in general and this proposition, that *Jesus is the Christ*, then they do not have as much communion with each other as two other Christians who both fear **GOD** and also understand the Holy Scripture in the same way—that is, sharing the Scripture and the **Sense** <note>original: "Zin"</note> of the Scripture alongside the understanding of all the tenets of religion. ## XIII.

->*On the Equality of the Members, and of the Overseer*<-
->*in Groningen.*<-

In Holland, all members have an equal say. However, in Groningen, things are arranged differently in this regard. For there, the Collegiants <term>Collegianten: A 17th-century Dutch religious movement that met in "colleges" to discuss scripture without formal clergy</term> have their Overseer, Elders, and Deacons, who are chosen for these roles by the full Brotherhood. These officials must, *First*, be good examples in both teaching and life. They must, *Secondly*, see to it that the arrangements established by the congregation are observed and maintained. And *Thirdly*, it is their duty to call the Brotherhood together; to receive, record, and—according to the instructions of the Brotherhood—apply the common funds; to take the votes, and so on. ### XIV.
### *Exclusion of Socinianism in Groningen.*

The Groningen Collegiants <term>Collegianten: A 17th-century Dutch religious movement that met in "colleges" to discuss scripture without formal clergy</term> may have no specific Creed <note>original: "Geloofsbelydenis"</note>, but nonetheless their Overseer <note>original: "Opziender"</note> claims, in a Justification which he has composed on behalf of his Brothers, that in his congregation, the teachings of Socinus <term>Socinianism: A non-trinitarian belief system founded by Fausto Sozzini which rejected the divinity of Christ and the traditional doctrine of the Trinity</term> and his followers (concerning the Holy Trinity, the Eternal Divinity of the Son, the Satisfaction of the Savior <note>The theological concept that Christ’s death satisfied God’s justice</note>, Justification through faith alone, and the like) are held to be grave errors. He asserts that one who harbors these views would only be tolerated as long as there was hope of setting him right; but that the group would dismiss him from the Brotherhood once he had become entrenched in those errors. 

This is, it seems, understood differently by the other Collegiants <note>Referring to the groups in Holland, such as in Amsterdam or Rijnsburg</note>: for they require nothing more than that one believes that Jesus is the Christ, the Source of Salvation; that one accepts the Scriptures as the Word of God; that one holds to no error condemned in Holy Scripture in express words (for example, the denial of the Resurrection of the Dead); and that one lives in no manifest works of the flesh. Consequently, they do not exclude the Socinians from the communion of their church. ### XV.

->*Of the Colleges.*<-

All the Collegiants <term>Collegianten: Members of a 17th- and 18th-century Dutch movement that valued individual Bible study and rejected formal church hierarchies</term> from all places gather together twice a year in Rijnsburg <note>Rijnsburg, near Leiden, served as the central meeting place for the group, famous for their large baptismal gatherings</note>. But the Collegiants who live near one another in the same city or place have, in addition to those two *Great and General Assemblies*, their own particular *Weekly Exercises*, in the city or place where they reside. And these they call Colleges or Exercises <term>Oeffeningen: "Exercises" or "meetings" where members could speak freely and interpret scripture without a minister</term>.

### XVII.

->*Of the Public Addresses at Rijnsburg, and the Provision for them.*<-

Arrangements were previously made by various Colleges in the neighborhood, in case no one should offer themselves spontaneously to bring the Word [*at Rijnsburg*] <note>The brackets indicate a clarification of where the speaking occurs—specifically at the central gathering place in Rijnsburg.</note> and to perform the Service. Thus, for every Address, a capable man is chosen; and this person, who is appointed in such a manner by the Brothers, is usually not preempted by anyone else. The five specific Assemblies—Rotterdam, Leiden, Amsterdam, Haarlem, and North Holland (under which various Colleges are included)—which care for the physical maintenance <note>This refers to the financial and logistical upkeep of the meeting houses and community needs.</note> of the Rijnsburg Assembly, also arrange the turns for these Addresses. There are, as we have seen, Five Religious Acts <term>Religious Acts: *Godsdienstige Handelingen*, refers here to the specific scheduled sessions of worship and speaking</term> performed: namely, the first on Saturday; the second on Sunday morning; the third during the Lord's Supper <term>Lord's Supper: *Avondmael*, the central communal meal and rite of the Collegiants</term> itself; the fourth on Sunday afternoon; and the fifth on Monday morning. And so, each of the aforementioned Colleges has something to provide. They alternate according to certain rotations. But each of these five companies chooses from among the persons who are among them one who has spoken at Rijnsburg before (for which they always take the most capable), and who

# XVIII.

## *Of the Nature of the Rijnsburg Assembly, and the Address before the Table.*

The character and nature of this Assembly, as well as to some extent the content of those speeches, consists mainly of the following. If one were to consider the distinct conceptions of men—which arise from different opinions, from a greater or lesser insight into and use of the Holy Scripture <note>original: *H. Schrift*</note>, from differences in nationality, from upbringing, and similar factors—one would easily find that men are not naturally suited for total agreement in matters of religion <note>original: *Godsdienft*</note>. Furthermore, it is an indubitable certainty that no person of reason <note>original: *Menfch van Verftand*</note> has the choice to form their own beliefs on matters of faith <note>original: *Geloofszaeken*</note> according to their own whim; rather, every individual must necessarily follow the guidance of their own understanding, even though they may be accustomed to changing their own views on many things over time. Likewise, one could not accuse anyone of erring intentionally in the weightiest matters. Add to this that it did not please the Most High to create men with one and the same mind and understanding, or to define religion so strictly that it would be impossible to differ from one another in it;

<summary>This page describes the long preparation required for those leading the Collegiant services and introduces a philosophical defense of religious pluralism based on the inherent diversity of human reason and upbringing.</summary>
<keywords>Rijnsburg Assembly, Holy Supper, religious tolerance, freedom of conscience, Holy Scripture, human understanding, Collegiants</keywords>
