although it would have been very easy for Him to bring all religions under a single rule of conduct <note>original: *Rigtfnoer*</note>, just as happens regarding other matters in which it was highly necessary for the best of human society: for example, that among all peoples, two and three together make five. The Most High **GOD**, and **JESUS**, who was perfect in all wisdom, did not see fit to leave behind an Infallibly Speaking Judge <term>Infallibly Speaking Judge: a reference to the Pope or a central ecclesiastical authority, which the Collegiants rejected in favor of individual conscience</term> in the Church, but directed everyone to the Revealed Word of Grace and their own conscience. Meanwhile, it remained unbreakably firm that the disciples of **JESUS** have Love and Unity as a livery <note>original: *liverei*; here meaning a distinctive uniform or identifying mark</note>. For that reason, it was highly necessary that one should tolerate and bear with one another, regardless of the diversity of opinions, just as one would wish to be tolerated and borne with oneself. And so one must, through the Bond of Tolerance, remain joined to one another in love; since it would certainly be loveless to condemn someone, and tyrannical to persecute him. Not that it was a matter of indifference to the Collegiants which opinions were held regarding the various points of religion. Certainly not: they wish to maintain in every way that one view promotes the honor of **GOD** and **JESUS CHRISTUS** more, and gives more occasion for the advancement of true virtue and the fear of God, than another. Nor is it their meaning that it would be absurd if each person, in the ecclesiastical household in which they find themselves and from which they do not need to depart, has a formulary of faith <note>original: *Geloofsformulier*; a formal statement of religious doctrine or a creed</note> for themselves; only one must be carefully on guard that one does not impose such on others as a

Therefore, on this basis, they offer the hand of Brotherhood to all Protestants (as even the Roman Catholic Christians exclude themselves, since they recognize a Visible Judge in Spiritual Matters <note>A reference to the Pope or the centralized Church hierarchy, which the Collegiants rejected</note>), as well as to all true Christians who confess that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the Living **GOD**, of whatever denomination they might be, so that at one and the same Table, over which Christ alone has command, they might openly testify through the use of the Holy Communion <term>Holy Communion: also called the Lord's Supper; the Collegiants practiced "open communion," inviting all believers regardless of their specific sect</term>, that they are all together members of Christ’s body, of which He—Blessed be He!—is the only Head; and that they might thus keep the unity of the Spirit through the Bond of Peace. They believe that this is the only way to heal again the pitiful schisms <note>original: *Scheuringen*</note> of Christendom. And that such a union is not impossible, they confirm with the example of the Jews, who in former times stood against one another in many disputes under the names of three main sects, and yet as brothers performed their worship in Jerusalem with one accord. It also seems to them to be a symbol, related to this, that one shall enter the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, through several gates. Even the Early Christian Church would serve as an example of how one, while holding different opinions, can be of one heart and one soul. They likewise declare and testify that they do not wish to hold the Lord’s Supper <term>Lord's Supper: known as *Avondmael* in Dutch, this was the central, often monthly, communal ritual of the Collegiants</term> with **wicked** men who live in sin, upon which damnation is pronounced in God’s Word; nevertheless, they leave it to each individual to examine themselves in this regard. On the contrary, they earnestly and strongly insist on the practice of true holiness and godliness, and on possessing the fruits of the Spirit—at the very least, that one, after sincere repentance and sorrow for one's sins, has surrendered oneself to faithfully serve the Most High from now on with the assistance of God’s Spirit. I have taken this entire observation from a small writing of a Collegiant, because many of the aims of these brothers appear therein; notwithstanding that I am well aware that the Collegiants today are accustomed to making their addresses before the use of the Lord’s Supper much more exhortatory in nature.

In the meantime, fourteen or fifteen Brothers (for that many can fit at the table), who sit closest, step forward without observing any rank. Often young people go along among the first, to show that no distinction is made there. Afterward, he also returns to his place; and the Ceremony is concluded with prayers and hymns.

### XXI.
### Of the Emotionality of the Speeches.

All the ecclesiastical speeches <term>Speeches: *Redevoeringen*; the Collegiants did not have formal sermons by ordained ministers, but rather "exhortations" or speeches by lay members</term> in Rijnsburg are free, and not bound to any specific Biblical lections. ### XXII.

### *Of the Great House in Rijnsburg.*

**T**he House in the east end of the Village is specifically called *the Great House*. It has not only a spacious perimeter of more than thirty rooms, but also a large Garden or Court, and besides that, a wide-stretching Alley or walking-path around it. It was established by a Collegiant individual with the aim that some friends coming from outside the village could take up residence there during the time of the Meetings. An open table is kept there for between sixty and seventy people, and they further sustain one another with Religious Exercises <term>Religious Exercises: *Godsdienstige Oeffeningen*; informal spiritual gatherings involving prayer, singing, and Bible study, distinct from formal church services</term> during the time of the Rijnsburg Gatherings. This House is actually a bequest <note>original: *Making*; a legacy or endowment</note> for the benefit of the Orphanage of the Collegiants in Amsterdam. The Regents of that Orphanage had first divided it into six dwellings and left it to six good friends by way of life annuities <term>Life annuities: *Lyfrenten*; a financial arrangement where an individual pays a lump sum in exchange for the right to live in or receive income from a property for the rest of their life</term> for a sum of three hundred guilders for each part. Those six persons used the House when they were in Rijnsburg and took people whom they liked with them into the empty rooms. However, meanwhile a change took place, and the House was sold in its entirety to some wealthy Collegiants, who not only take up residence there themselves but also fill the remaining rooms with good friends.

## XXIII.
### *Of the Baptismal Bath.*

<insert>In the year 1736, a square baptismal bath was dug.</insert> One can let as much warm water from a kettle, which stands nearby, into the baptismal bath as is required. This place of baptism is not located by the meeting house, or, if I may speak so, by the church of the Rijnsburgers, but by the aforementioned Great House. For the Collegiants <term>Collegiants: A Dutch Protestant group known for their lack of formal clergy and their emphasis on individual interpretation and tolerance</term> do not wish for this manner of baptizing to be regarded as an essential <term>essential: *wezendlyk*; a fundamental or core requirement</term> part of their assembly; noting that they count among them people who either make no account of baptism at all, or insist upon infant baptism, or consider immersion <term>immersion: *onderdompeling*; the practice of submerging the entire body in water, as opposed to sprinkling</term> to be unnecessary.

## XXIV.
### *Of the Manner of Baptizing There.*

Many meetings pass by before one person or another is baptized. But when a baptism does take place, the baptizer stands near the baptismal bath and offers a prayer under the open sky. Whereupon he descends the steps into the bath with the person to be baptized. The candidate kneels down, and the water reaches up to his throat; but the baptizer stands upright in the water, <insert>and he dips the head of the candidate under the water, while pronouncing the words of institution.</insert> <note>original: *woorden der Instellinge*; referring to the traditional formula: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit."</note>

### XXVII.

The outward worship in the Colleges <term>Colleges: *Collegiën*; the small, informal groups from which the "Collegiants" took their name</term> is practiced in the following order. First, there is singing; then a brother <note>Collegiants referred to one another as "Brothers," emphasizing their rejection of formal clerical titles like "Minister" or "Priest."</note> prays while standing and speaking aloud. When that is finished, the First Speaker (*) reads the Scripture passage and explains it as learnedly as is possible for him. ### XXVIII.

#### *Of the Songs and Hymns of the Rhynsburgers.* <note>The Collegiants were often called Rhynsburgers because their most important biannual meetings took place in the village of Rijnsburg.</note>

The Collegiants boast that their outward religious practice, with respect to singing, is considerably better arranged than in any other party of the Dutch churches. And they are right. For among all the denominations <term>Denominations: *Gezindheden*; the various religious groups in the Dutch Republic, such as the Reformed, Mennonites, or Lutherans</term>, one keeps to the Psalms of David, which were rhymed long ago, and there are but few hymns which have been translated into the Dutch language in the Evangelical-Lutheran Church. But the Collegiants have excellent spiritual songs, which were composed by some of their Brothers as well as by other fellow believers in earlier times. They have thus not only set the Psalms of King David into edifying rhymes, and made them more suited to the circumstances of the present times, by the famous **Dirk Rafaëlsz. Kamphuizen** <note>A famous poet and artist (1586–1627) whose "Edifying Rhymes" were staples of Dutch non-conformist piety</note>, but they also have many other hymns; as for example, the same **Kamphuizen**’s *Edifying Rhymes*, [along with the Psalms] in two volumes; likewise Dr. **Reinier Rooleeuw**’s *Edifying Hymns*; and furthermore, the *Pleasure-Garden of the Soul* <term>Pleasure-Garden of the Soul: *Lufthof der Ziele*; a poetic title for a collection of hymns meant to provide spiritual delight and rest</term>, composed by various authors and collected by **Klaes Stapel**.

## XXXI.

### XXXII.
### *Regarding the Ecclesiastical Revenues of the Collegiants.*

In former times, the Collegiants had no specific or established funds <term>Funds: *Kassen*; literally "chests" or treasuries used to hold communal money</term> which drew their income and supply from permanent and fixed capital or properties. They feared that if they possessed wealthy so-called "church properties," all sorts of people might join them with the wrong intentions <note>The Collegiants were wary of "bread-protestants"—people who joined a religious group specifically to benefit from its welfare or charity systems</note>; it also hindered them because they did not see how they could manage in such a case without appointing Deacons <term>Deacons: *Diakonen*; church officers typically charged with the care of the poor and financial administration</term>. For they were opposed to ecclesiastical offices and appointments, and could by no means bring themselves to this. For that reason, only the wealthy Brothers <note>original: *Broeders*; a term used to address fellow members of the community</note> were gathered and requested from time to time to contribute something toward the common need according to their own discretion. This they did; and it was left to one of them to spend and distribute these alms <note>original: *Aelmoessen*</note>. When these were exhausted, this person would give an account of his expenditures to the Friends who had donated; and, if it was found necessary, a new supply was gathered together once more. —

To this type of expenditure also belongs the funding for the Bread and Wine required for the Lord's Supper <term>Lord's Supper: *Avondmael*; the communal meal of bread and wine practiced by the group</term>, which the Amsterdam Collegiants hold annually among themselves in their meeting place in the orphanage there, and which is usually held on the last Sunday of January.

*Secondly*, this fund serves to fulfill the needs of poor Collegiants, who are assisted with alms.

*Thirdly*, it serves to help other Collegiants who are indeed able to earn a living and do not desire alms, but who nevertheless require an advance of some money for the continuation and improvement of their livelihood and business. To such individuals, some money is lent from this fund, generally without any interest, provided that they are obligated to repay the advanced principal at the appointed time. This praiseworthy arrangement, however, extends only to cases of necessity: thus, a merchant who needs money for a large enterprise would not find success here; no, this is intended only for tradesmen <term>Tradesmen: *Ambagtsluiden*; skilled manual workers or artisans</term> and others who wish to start their own household or a kind of shop, and the like. One lends someone a maximum of one thousand Guilders <note original="Duizend Guldens">1,000 Dutch guilders was a significant sum in the 18th century, enough to set up a modest workshop or business</note>.

*Fourthly*, from this fund, alms are also distributed to other fellow believers, regardless of which denomination <term>Denomination: *Gezindheit*; a term used to describe different religious groups or sects</term> they belong to, in times of urgent need; and this is done both for entire congregations and for private individuals.

<meta>catchword: But</meta>

But this must be understood in the following way. In the room where the Collegiants meet, a special Poor Box has been placed with this inscription: *For the Common Poor.* Whatever is placed inside forms a separate fund for the poor of all denominations <note>The Collegiants were noted for their "horizontal" or non-sectarian charity, aiding those outside their own circle</note>; and if this is insufficient, it is supplemented from the aforementioned Large Fund. One must not imagine, however, that all beggars could simply run here to get money: those who receive anything must be truly needy and worthy of alms.

The Fund of the Collegiants in Amsterdam has not yet obtained the privilege of being recognized as spiritual or ecclesiastical property, namely, the freedom from taxes and duties; except that the government, regarding a certain special inheritance <term>Inheritance: *Erf-Making*; a bequest or legacy left in a will</term> that recently fell to this fund, waived the usual deduction for the benefit of the country of its own accord, just as it is accustomed to do regarding legacies and bequests to other churches. This fund has not yet been in such a state that it required this privilege. But there is no doubt that it would, upon a properly submitted request, obtain such.

## XXXIV.

### *Whether the Collegiants are a distinct Denomination.*

Many of the members of this assembly belong to the Remonstrants, or to the Mennonites <term>Mennonites: *Doopsgezinden*; literally "baptism-minded," a Protestant group practicing believer's baptism and non-violence</term>, whom I have previously called "Remonstrant-minded." They can do this: for the Remonstrants, Remonstrant Mennonites, and Collegiants do not exclude one another from mutual participation in the Lord’s Supper, etc. One even finds several among the Mennonite teachers who are simultaneously Collegiants. ### XXXV.

->*Of their Freedom and Peace.*<-

As far as we know, the Collegiants in Holland have enjoyed Peace and Freedom for a long time. But in Groningen, they were disturbed at the beginning of this Century, because a Reformed inhabitant had joined their Company, whose Wife viewed this as a very bad thing and therefore turned to one of her Ministers <term>Ministers: *Predikanten*; specifically referring to the ordained clergy of the state-sanctioned Reformed Church</term>. It is said that he once went with that woman into the Meeting-house and took the Bible out of the hands of the aforementioned Man, who at that moment was delivering the discourse among the Brothers, and in his place gave the public Declaration, which he claimed belonged to him and other Called Teachers <term>Called Teachers: *Beroepen Leeraers*; professional, ordained clergy who were "called" by a specific congregation, unlike the lay-speakers of the Collegiants</term> alone. Because of this, the Benches were removed from their Meeting-house, and a fine was imposed upon the Collegiants. However, they soon managed to obtain peace again. One could also mention here to some extent that once in Leiden and in Amsterdam their Meet-
